title: LLM Reasoning Series: Generators, Verifiers, and Test-Time Selection
text:
2026-06-06
Multi-step mathematical reasoning is a setting where autoregressive language models frequently fail. A single error early in a solution propagates and is not corrected, so a model that is individually competent at each step can still produce a wrong final answer. The paper addresses this problem with two contributions (Cobbe et al. 2021). The first is GSM8K, a dataset of 8.5K grade-school math word problems with natural-language solutions, designed as a benchmark for informal reasoning. The second is a verification method: instead of generating one solution, the model generates many candidate solutions, and a separately trained verifier scores them so that the highest-scoring candidate can be selected.

title: LLM Reasoning Series: Generators, Verifiers, and Test-Time Selection
text:
1 The GSM8K Dataset
GSM8K consists of 8.5K grade-school math word problems written by human contributors, split into 7.5K training and 1K test problems (Cobbe et al. 2021). Each problem requires between two and eight steps and uses elementary arithmetic operations. Solutions are written in natural language rather than as equations alone.
The dataset is built around four design principles:

High quality. Problems are human-written rather than scraped. After agreement checks in which contributors re-solve each other’s problems, the estimated rate of breaking errors is about 1.7%.
High diversity. Templated problems are avoided, so problems differ in linguistic form and scenario rather than superficial detail. Held-out accuracy then measures generalization rather than memorization.
Moderate difficulty. Difficulty is calibrated to be hard for the largest available models without being intractable, so the dataset can resolve differences in data-scaling between methods.
Natural-language solutions. Solutions are collected as natural-language explanations rather than pure expressions.

These properties determine what the benchmark measures. Because problems are diverse and untemplated, held-out accuracy reflects generalization. Because difficulty is calibrated to the capability of large models, the benchmark resolves differences between methods that would be invisible on a dataset that is either saturated or intractable.
To reduce arithmetic mistakes, all models are trained to use a calculator through calculation annotations injected into the training data. At test time, sampling is overridden when the model emits a well-formed annotation, and the expression is evaluated directly.

title: LLM Reasoning Series: Generators, Verifiers, and Test-Time Selection
section: 2 The Finetuning Baseline and Its Scaling Behavior
text:
2 The Finetuning Baseline and Its Scaling Behavior
The baseline method is autoregressive finetuning on the demonstrations, evaluated by a single low-temperature sample per test problem (Cobbe et al. 2021). Across model sizes the test solve rate is approximately log-linear. Extrapolating this trend, attainment of an 80\% solve rate by finetuning alone would require a model of order 10^{16} parameters, or the 175B model trained on at least two additional orders of magnitude of data.
The slope is shallow because autoregressive decoding has no error-correction mechanism. A model writing a multi-step derivation cannot revise an earlier step, so an early error propagates and the probability of a fully correct solution decreases multiplicatively in the number of steps. Raising single-sample accuracy requires reducing the per-step error rate across the entire trajectory.
The intermediate reasoning is necessary, not optional. A 6B model finetuned to emit only the final answer, with no intermediate steps, attains a solve rate of 5.2\%, compared with 20.6\% for the same model when it generates the full natural-language solution (Cobbe et al. 2021).

title: LLM Reasoning Series: Generators, Verifiers, and Test-Time Selection
text:
3 Sampling Coverage: The test@N Metric
Allowing N samples per problem changes the relevant quantity. Define test@N as the fraction of problems for which at least one of N samples is correct. If a single sample solves problem x with probability p_\theta(x) and the samples are independent, then

\text{test@}N \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{x}\!\left[\, 1 - \big(1 - p_\theta(x)\big)^{N} \,\right].

The expression is written as the complement of joint failure because “at least one of N samples is correct” is the negation of “all N samples are incorrect,” and under independence the probability that all fail is (1 - p_\theta)^N. This form makes the effect of N explicit. A problem solved with per-sample probability 0.05 is solved at least once across 100 samples with probability 1 - 0.95^{100} \approx 0.994. A correct solution is therefore usually present in the sample set even when the generator does not assign it the highest probability on a single greedy draw. This difference between producing a correct solution and producing one as the single most probable output is what the verification method exploits.
The independence assumption is an idealization, and the paper relies on its consequences without stating it. Samples drawn from one model at a fixed temperature are correlated. A model whose output distribution has concentrated retains a high per-sample p_\theta but generates few distinct solutions, so its effective sample count is below N. The training procedure that controls this concentration is discussed below.

title: LLM Reasoning Series: Generators, Verifiers, and Test-Time Selection
text:
4 The Verification Pipeline
The verification method has three steps (Cobbe et al. 2021):

Finetune a generator on the training set for two epochs.
Sample 100 completions per training problem and label each as correct or incorrect according solely to whether its final answer matches.
Train a verifier for one epoch to predict this correctness label.

At test time, the generator produces multiple completions, the verifier scores each, and the highest-scoring completion is returned. The labels are produced by arithmetic comparison of the final answer rather than by human annotation, which is what allows the verifier’s training data to scale.
The two-epoch limit on generator training follows from the coverage metric. Extended generator training increases single-sample accuracy, but test@100 peaks within the first few epochs and then declines as the output distribution concentrates and sample diversity falls (Cobbe et al. 2021). The verifier selects only among supplied candidates, so it requires a generator with high coverage rather than high single-sample accuracy. Stopping generator training early preserves the count of distinct samples on which selection depends.
The relative size of the two models is also informative. A large generator paired with a small verifier outperforms a small generator paired with a large verifier (Cobbe et al. 2021). Candidate coverage contributes more to final accuracy than verifier capacity. A verifier substantially smaller than its generator remains effective, which indicates that it is not performing complete step-by-step verification — a small model lacks the capacity for that — but is instead using shallow features that correlate with correct answers. This property is relevant to the test-time behavior described below.

title: LLM Reasoning Series: Generators, Verifiers, and Test-Time Selection
text:
5 Token-Level and Solution-Level Verifiers
The default verifier emits a prediction after each token rather than a single prediction for the completed solution:

V\big(x,\, y_{\le t}\big) \;\approx\; P\big(\text{final answer correct} \mid x,\, y_{\le t}\big).

This token-level form is a value function over the partial solution. It trains more slowly and with more noise than the solution-level variant, which scores only the completed answer, but it reaches higher final performance and continues to improve while the solution-level variant overfits (Cobbe et al. 2021). Predicting at every prefix requires the model to evaluate the solution as it develops rather than only at the final answer.
The supervision is outcome-based. Each token in a solution receives the single label of final-answer correctness, applied to all positions. Under the standard taxonomy this verifier is an outcome reward model; it is the reference instance against which later process-supervised methods are compared. A process reward model is defined by training on per-step labels that distinguish correct from incorrect steps within a solution, including solutions that reach the correct final answer. This verifier has no such labels, so the token-level prediction adds density of output rather than step-level supervision. Later work supplies the missing labels directly: Lightman et al. train a process reward model on human step-level annotations and release PRM800K, a dataset of 800,000 such labels, reporting that process supervision outperforms outcome supervision on the MATH dataset (Lightman et al. 2023).
This supervision carries a known limitation. A solution that reaches the correct final answer through incorrect reasoning is labeled correct, which produces false positives that per-token prediction cannot resolve, because the labels do not encode step correctness. The verifier is also trained with an auxiliary language-modeling objective alongside the correctness objective; the paper reports this as a consistent improvement, attributable to better modeling of the solution distribution.

title: LLM Reasoning Series: Generators, Verifiers, and Test-Time Selection
text:
6 Test-Time Sample Count and Voting
At test time the selection rule is

\hat{y} \;=\; \arg\max_{i \in \{1,\dots,N\}} V\big(x,\, y_i\big),

the highest-scoring of N samples. The achievable accuracy is bounded above by test@N, because the verifier cannot select a correct solution that was never sampled, and the verifier determines how much of that bound is realized. For moderate N, increasing N raises both the bound and the realized accuracy.
The relation does not hold for large N. Increasing the number of completions improves accuracy up to approximately 400 per problem, after which accuracy declines (Cobbe et al. 2021). The paper attributes this to the selection of “adversarial solutions that fool the verifier”: because the verifier is an estimator of correctness rather than correctness itself, searching over more samples eventually selects solutions that the verifier scores highly but that are not correct. This behavior was later described in terms of reward over-optimization; the paper documents the phenomenon without using that terminology.
One mitigation is to take a majority vote over the highest-ranked candidates rather than selecting the single maximum. With 100 samples, a vote over the top 3–5 candidates is approximately optimal; with 3,200 samples, a vote over the top 30 (Cobbe et al. 2021). A single high-scoring incorrect solution can attain the maximum verifier score but rarely forms a plurality of final answers, so aggregating over several high-ranked candidates reduces sensitivity to the verifier’s largest single error.

title: LLM Reasoning Series: Generators, Verifiers, and Test-Time Selection
text:
7 Regularization with Dropout
Both finetuning and verification benefit from residual dropout, applied at a rate of 20% (Cobbe et al. 2021). The largest effect is on the solution-level verifier, where dropout reduces overfitting to approximately the performance of the token-level verifier. The improvement is smaller for the token-level verifier, which overfits less to begin with. Across the paper’s results, the recurring failure mode is concentration of the model on the single correct answer with loss of the diversity that selection requires, and each technique — the two-epoch generator, the token-level value function, and dropout — counteracts it.

title: LLM Reasoning Series: Generators, Verifiers, and Test-Time Selection
text:
8 Putting It Together
The paper introduces GSM8K and a verification method for grade-school math reasoning. Finetuning a generator and evaluating a single sample improves only slowly with data and model size. The verification method instead generates many candidate solutions and selects among them with a learned verifier, which is trained on outcome labels derived automatically from final-answer correctness. The token-level verifier is an outcome reward model that predicts correctness after each token. On the full dataset, 6B verification slightly exceeds a finetuned 175B model, a difference the paper characterizes as approximately a 30x increase in model size, and verification improves with data faster than the finetuning baseline.
The method also has measurable limits. Accuracy from additional test-time samples increases only up to a point, beyond which selection begins to favor solutions that the verifier scores highly without being correct. The combination of a supervised generator, a learned verifier, and selection over many samples at test time recurs in later work on reasoning systems (DeepSeek-AI et al. 2025; Shao et al. 2024).

title: LLM Alignment Series: Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback
text:
2026-05-25
Google DeepMind’s Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback (RLAIF) study lands a clean answer to a question about labels: swap the human annotators behind RLHF for an off-the-shelf language model, and across summarization and two dialogue tasks the resulting policy is preferred by humans at statistically indistinguishable rates, with a coin-flip outcome head-to-head (Lee et al. 2024). That is a real result, and it is the smaller of the two findings in the report.
The larger finding sits a layer down, in a component both pipelines kept without questioning. The trained reward model is the disposable link in the alignment chain. Three results converge on that conclusion: RLAIF matches RLHF while running on a reward model measurably less accurate against human preferences; reward-model accuracy fails to predict which policy you end up with; and direct-RLAIF, the paper’s own strongest method, deletes the reward model outright and beats the version that keeps it. These are not three curiosities but one observation seen from three angles — and the reasons RLAIF can match RLHF turn out to be the same reasons the reward model can be thrown away.

title: LLM Alignment Series: Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback
text:
1 One Pipeline, One Swapped Part
The comparison only means something if the two systems differ in exactly one place, and the design is disciplined about this. Both arms start from the same supervised checkpoint, PaLM 2 XS. Both train a reward model on a preference dataset. Both then optimize the same objective with the same algorithm. The single difference is who labeled the preferences — a human, or an instruction-tuned PaLM 2 L asked to pick the better of two candidates.
The objective they share is the experiment’s control, so it is worth writing out:

J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}\Big[(1-\beta)\,r_\phi(y\mid x) - \beta\,D_{KL}\big(\pi^{RL}_\theta(y\mid x)\,\|\,\pi^{SFT}(y\mid x)\big)\Big]

The first term pulls the policy toward whatever the reward model rewards. The KL term leashes it to the supervised policy so it cannot drift into the high-reward, low-quality region where reward hacking lives. Why express the trade-off as the convex blend (1-\beta) and \beta rather than reward-minus-penalty with a free multiplier? Because tying the two coefficients together bounds the objective: at \beta=1 you optimize pure imitation, at \beta=0 pure reward, and every setting in between is a genuine interpolation rather than two knobs that can fight each other. Fixing this objective, \beta, and the optimizer across both arms is what licenses the causal reading — any downstream difference is attributable to the reward source, not the recipe. One detail to flag: the optimizer is REINFORCE with a baseline, not PPO. That raises the bar on the human-feedback side rather than lowering it, since a weaker optimizer that still lets AI feedback keep pace makes the parity result more conservative, not less.
On that footing the headline numbers land where the abstract promises. RLAIF and RLHF beat the supervised baseline 71% and 73% of the time on summarization, 63% and 64% on helpful dialogue, and sit at 50% and 52% against each other. On harmlessness, RLAIF separates from the pack with an 88% harmless rate against RLHF’s 76%.

title: LLM Alignment Series: Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback
section: 2 “Comparable” Is Partly a Statement About Human Noise
text:
2 “Comparable” Is Partly a Statement About Human Noise
Before reading parity as a triumph, ask what the ceiling is. The summarization preferences come from a dataset whose human inter-annotator agreement was estimated at 73–77%. Hold that against the best AI labeler’s alignment with human preferences: 78%. The model agrees with a held-out human about as often as humans agree with each other.
That reframes “comparable.” Two labelers that each match a human roughly three-quarters of the time will, almost mechanically, yield reward signals of similar quality, because the target they chase is itself noisy. When ground truth behaves like a coin weighted 75/25, the difference between a 78%-accurate rater and a 77%-accurate rater disappears into sampling error. RLAIF matching RLHF is therefore partly a fact about RLAIF and partly a fact about how loose the human signal was to begin with.
This does not dissolve the practical claim — if the human ceiling is where it is, an AI labeler that reaches it is good enough for the job. But it sharpens what “good enough” means. It is not that AI feedback has closed the gap to some ideal human judgment; it is that the human judgment being approximated was already saturated with disagreement, so any rater landing inside that band looks equivalent. The honest version of the result is conditional: for tasks where humans agree only 73–77% of the time, AI labels are competitive. On a task with crisper ground truth, the story could break differently, and nothing here forecloses that.

title: LLM Alignment Series: Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback
section: 3 Two Ways to Turn an Opinion Into a Reward
text:
3 Two Ways to Turn an Opinion Into a Reward
How the labeler’s judgment becomes a training signal is where the paper’s instincts show, and it sets up the d-RLAIF result.
Canonical RLAIF still trains a reward model, but not with the loss everyone reaches for first. The standard objective is the Bradley–Terry pairwise log-likelihood,

\mathcal{L}_r(\phi) = -\mathbb{E}_{(x,y_w,y_l)\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\log\sigma\big(r_\phi(x,y_w)-r_\phi(x,y_l)\big)\right],

which treats each datum as a hard verdict: y_w beat y_l, end of story. The LLM labeler does not give a verdict. It gives a distribution — the softmax over the log-probabilities of generating the tokens “1” and “2” — that might read [0.6, 0.4]. So RLAIF instead trains the reward model with a cross-entropy loss against the softmax of its own scores, matching the labeler’s confidence, not just its argmax. The authors name this plainly: it is distillation.
Why keep the soft target? Because hard-thresholding [0.6, 0.4] to [1,0] before training discards exactly what makes a fallible labeler usable. A 51/49 near-tie and a 99/1 near-certainty would then push the reward model with identical force, though one is essentially a coin flip. The soft label lets low-confidence pairs move the reward model less — label smoothing for free, which the pairwise loss cannot express. Read against the ceiling argument, this is more than a tidiness point: a soft label is the labeler honestly reporting that it, too, is unsure, which on a 75%-agreement task is the correct posture.
Direct-RLAIF presses the same instinct to its conclusion and asks why the reward model needs to exist. Rather than distilling preferences into a network once and freezing it, d-RLAIF prompts the labeler to score a single response on a 1–10 scale during RL and reads the reward off the token distribution,

s(y \mid x) = \sum_{i=1}^{10} i \cdot P(i \mid y, x),

then rescales to [-1,1]. Taking the expectation rather than the argmax is the whole move. Decode the single most likely score and you get one of ten integers — a step function whose flat plateaus give RL nothing to climb between levels. The probability-weighted mean is continuous: mass split between “7” and “8” returns 7.5 instead of snapping to whichever token wins by an epsilon. A discrete rating becomes a smooth reward surface, which is the only reason it can sit inside a gradient-based loop at all.

title: LLM Alignment Series: Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback
section: 4 Why Throwing the Reward Model Out Helps
text:
4 Why Throwing the Reward Model Out Helps
The reason d-RLAIF gives for itself is staleness. A reward model is trained once, on responses sampled from the initial policy. As RL moves the policy, its outputs drift from that training distribution, and the reward model is increasingly asked to score things unlike anything it saw. Its judgments rot precisely where you now need them.
The paper states this but leaves the key subtlety implicit, and it is the subtlety that explains why the fix works. A frozen off-the-shelf scorer also has fixed weights, so why is it immune? Because staleness was never about the weights. It was about the training distribution being fixed. The reward model was narrowly fit to one policy’s outputs; the off-the-shelf labeler was never fit to the policy at all. As a generalist rater, it does not experience the policy’s distributional shift as out-of-distribution the way a model trained to mimic preferences over a single, now-obsolete sampling distribution does. The immunity is to distributional drift, not to weight staleness — and that is the actual engine of the result.
So the generalist beats the specialist. Shown responses side by side, annotators prefer d-RLAIF over a same-size canonical RLAIF policy 60% of the time, and d-RLAIF’s 74% win rate over the supervised baseline on summarization edges past canonical RLAIF’s. The reward model was not merely removable; keeping it was costing performance.

title: LLM Alignment Series: Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback
text:
5 The Crack the Paper Half-Acknowledges
Here is the result I think the authors undersold, because it reframes everything above. Reward-model accuracy does not predict the policy you get.
Against held-out human preferences, the human-feedback reward model scores 79.3% on summarization and the AI-feedback one only 74.2%. By the usual logic the human reward model should yield the better policy. It does not — RLAIF ties or wins. The inversion sharpens inside the AI-feedback setups: a reward model trained on plain “Base 0-shot” labels is more accurate (77.9%) than one trained on elaborate “Detailed + CoT” labels (74.2%), yet the more accurate reward model produces the worse policy after RL. The paper concedes, in a single appendix sentence, that reward-model accuracy “may not accurately reflect a RM’s effectiveness.”
That concession deserved to be a heading, not a footnote, because it is the premise the whole d-RLAIF result stands on. If top-1 ranking accuracy on a static human holdout fails to track the quality of the policy you train, the reward model is a leaky proxy being scored against the wrong yardstick. What predicts the policy is not how often the reward model ranks a frozen pair correctly; it is the shape and calibration of the reward surface over the moving distribution the policy actually explores. A reward model is a snapshot of preferences over yesterday’s outputs. A live labeler scores today’s. Once you see that gap, deleting the reward model stops looking like an efficiency hack and starts looking like the right response to a measurement that was misleading you.

title: LLM Alignment Series: Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback
section: 6 The Negative Results Carry More Information Than the Wins
text:
6 The Negative Results Carry More Information Than the Wins
The prompting-techniques study reads like routine ablation — try detailed instructions, chain-of-thought, few-shot exemplars, report the alignment numbers. The wins are tiny, under two points each. But the pattern of failures says more than the size of the wins, and reading it requires the metric being optimized: AI labeler alignment, how often the labeler agrees with a held-out human. For D examples,

z_{acc} = \frac{1}{D}\sum_{i=1}^{D} \mathbb{1}\left[\arg\max_j P^{AI}_{i,j} = p^H_i\right],

where P^{AI} is the matrix of soft AI preferences and p^H the vector of human labels. The form is deliberately cheap: it collapses the soft AI distribution back to a hard argmax and compares it to a hard human label, discarding the very calibration that soft-label distillation tried to preserve. That is the point — this number scores the labeler, not the policy, so it can be computed without an RL run. It is the dial the authors turn while iterating on prompts, because the real objective costs a full training run and a human study to read. It is a proxy for a proxy, and the failures are most legible with that in mind.
Three stand out. Chain-of-thought helps consistently on summarization, inconsistently elsewhere. Few-shot prompting hurts: on summarization and helpfulness, alignment falls as exemplars are added, and ten trials with different randomly drawn exemplars failed to beat zero-shot. Self-consistency — sampling several rationales and averaging — strictly degrades alignment, by over five points at the highest temperature.
These rhyme. The interventions that help a weak model reason through an unfamiliar task — worked examples, multiple sampled rationales — backfire when the model already has the task cold. The coherent reading is that an instruction-tuned PaLM 2 L already holds a well-formed notion of a good summary, so exemplars inject noise into a judgment it would otherwise make cleanly. This is the human-agreement ceiling seen from the labeler’s side: the task is easy enough and the model capable enough that the binding constraint is the target’s irreducible noise, not the model’s reasoning. You cannot prompt past a ceiling set by how much humans disagree.
One mechanical source of noise is worth a paragraph: position bias, the labeler’s tendency to favor a candidate by its slot. The fix is to run each pair twice with the order flipped and average. It works for the large labeler — PaLM 2 L prefers a fixed slot only 18% of the time — and patches over the small ones, where PaLM 2 XS prefers a fixed slot 56% of the time and, when it does, picks the second candidate 99% of the time. Averaging cancels a symmetric offset, but a 99%-directional thumb on the scale is not symmetric, so a residual survives — and it survives largest for exactly the small labelers the self-improvement story leans on.

title: LLM Alignment Series: Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback
section: 7 What the Cost Argument Buys, and Where “Scaling” Is Earned
text:
7 What the Cost Argument Buys, and Where “Scaling” Is Earned
The economic case is the paper’s cleanest claim and its easiest to over-read. Priced against contemporary GPT-4 and cloud-annotation rates, the estimate is roughly six cents per AI-labeled example against about sixty-seven cents per human one — over 10× cheaper, even after doubling the AI cost to pay for the position-bias double inference. The caveats are stated honestly: the figure excludes setup cost, annotator training, and the expert-versus-crowd distinction, and the authors reserve trained human experts as the gold standard for high-stakes domains. The 10× is throughput economics for crowd-grade labeling, not a claim that AI labels are free or expert-equivalent.
The structural point is the one the title’s “scaling” actually earns. For canonical RLAIF the labeler is called once, to build the dataset, and never again — the reward model carries the signal through RL. So the labeler’s cost amortizes over the whole run, which means a much larger labeler is not prohibitive, and the size results (alignment climbing 62.7% → 73.8% → 78% from XS to S to L) imply a bigger one would buy better labels. That is a genuine, monotone scaling curve the pipeline structure makes cheap to climb. d-RLAIF spends the advantage differently, calling the labeler at every step in exchange for freshness — the cost-side mirror of the staleness-versus-distillation trade.

title: LLM Alignment Series: Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback
section: 8 Where the Framing Outruns the Evidence
text:
8 Where the Framing Outruns the Evidence
The parity claim leans on its statistics harder than it admits. “Not statistically significantly different from 50%” is evidence that no gap was detected, not evidence of equality. With around 2,000 rating instances and three raters each the study is decently powered, but it never runs an equivalence test — the tool that would actually license “equally preferred.” The harmlessness win, which is significant, does quiet work to prop up “at least as good.” On the other two tasks the defensible statement is “we could not tell them apart,” which is weaker than parity even if it points the same way for a practitioner.
The harmlessness win itself rests partly on a change of instrument. Harmlessness is scored not by pairwise win rate but by independent harmful/harmless judgments, because too many responses were equally safe to rank. A more sensitive instrument can register an absolute gap a forced ranking washes out; layer on a labeler shaped heavily toward safety by instruction tuning, and the cleanest reading is that the metric change made the gap visible while the safety tuning made it real. Neither is a flaw, but “RLAIF is safer” is doing two jobs at once.
Then there is “self-improvement.” The authors are candid that the same-size case — labeler and policy at the same scale but different checkpoints — is not strict self-improvement. The strict case, on helpful dialogue, is real: the labeler and the initial policy are one checkpoint. Even there I would resist the phrase. Nothing is created from nothing. RL surfaces preference knowledge the base model already encodes but cannot express through its own sampling — the familiar gap between being able to rank two responses and being able to generate the better one. d-RLAIF converts the latent evaluator into a better sampler, which is useful and bounded: alignment falls from 78% to 62.7% as the rater shrinks, exactly what you expect if a model cannot bootstrap past its own evaluative ceiling. “Self-distillation up to the limit of what the model can already judge” is the more defensible label.
A last number keeps the win rates honest. RLAIF and RLHF generate longer responses than the baseline, and length flatters raters. After a post-hoc length correction the summarization gains over the baseline drop from 71%/73% to 59%/61% — about a third of the apparent improvement was length. The relative claim survives, since the correction hits both arms symmetrically and RLAIF-versus-RLHF stays a coin flip; the absolute claim takes the haircut. The authors admit the regression-based fix is imperfect and that a length-penalized training objective would be the principled experiment — which for a comparative paper is fine, but for anyone reading 71% as a quality score is a warning label.

title: LLM Alignment Series: Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback
text:
9 What the Paper Actually Moved
Stripped to its load-bearing wall, the contribution is not “AI feedback works” — Constitutional AI had already shown LLM-generated signal could drive RL (Bai et al. 2022). What this paper adds is the controlled isolation of the label source the earlier blend never allowed, and, more lastingly, a stack of evidence that the trained reward model is the soft spot in the pipeline the field built around InstructGPT (Ouyang et al. 2022).
The pieces only cohere when you stop reading them as separate ablations. The human-agreement ceiling explains why AI labels can compete at all: the target is noisy enough that a capable model lands inside the band of human disagreement. The prompting failures explain why you cannot squeeze much more from the labeler: it already knows the easy tasks. The accuracy disconnect explains why the obvious quality metric misleads. And d-RLAIF is what you build once you believe all three — a live judge in place of a frozen, drifting proxy.
DPO attacked the same pipeline from the optimizer side, folding the reward model into a classification loss (Rafailov et al. 2024). d-RLAIF attacks it from the reward side, keeping RL but swapping the frozen proxy for a live judge. Both circle one suspicion: the reward model was a convenience of 2020-era pipelines, and once the labeler is itself a capable model, that convenience is no longer worth its cost in staleness and lost calibration. The label-source debate got the title. The reward model’s expendability is what the years since went on to confirm.

title: Agentic AI Series: SWE-bench
Agentic AI Series: SWE-bench
text:
1 Introduction
Most code benchmarks are too simplified to reflect real software engineering. They usually evaluate models on short, self-contained tasks such as function completion or small code generation problems. Real GitHub issues are different. Solving them often requires navigating a large repository, identifying the relevant files, understanding cross-file dependencies, modifying multiple functions, and validating the fix through tests.
SWE-bench (Jimenez et al. 2024) was proposed to evaluate language models in this more realistic setting. Instead of asking whether a model can write a short snippet, it asks whether the model can resolve an actual GitHub issue. The setup is simple: given a repository snapshot and an issue description, the model must generate a patch, and the patch is judged by whether it makes the repository’s tests pass.
The benchmark contains 2,294 task instances drawn from 12 popular Python repositories. Each instance is based on a real GitHub issue and its corresponding merged pull request. To build the dataset, the authors first collect issue-linked pull requests, then retain those that genuinely resolve the issue and modify tests, and finally apply execution-level filtering to ensure that at least one test changes from failing to passing. This design makes the benchmark both realistic and automatically verifiable.
A central contribution of the paper is to show why this task is difficult. The issue descriptions are often long, the repositories are large, and the reference fixes frequently span multiple files. As a result, success on SWE-bench requires more than code generation. It also requires repository-level retrieval, long-context reasoning, cross-file understanding, patch generation, and execution-based verification.
The paper also introduces an open baseline model, SWE-Llama, trained on roughly 19,000 issue–pull request pairs by supervised fine-tuning CodeLlama 7B and 13B. This provides a reproducible reference point for future work. However, the most striking result is that even the strongest models at the time performed very poorly. Under BM25 retrieval, Claude 2 solved only about 1.96% of the tasks, and even idealized retrieval improved performance only modestly. The conclusion is clear: automatically resolving real repository-level issues remains a difficult but important problem for language models.

title: Agentic AI Series: SWE-bench
text:
2 What is SWE-bench
SWE-bench is constructed through a three-stage pipeline designed to convert noisy GitHub activity into executable software engineering tasks. The benchmark begins with pull requests drawn from 12 popular Python repositories and progressively filters them until the remaining instances are both realistic and behaviorally verifiable. This process reduces roughly 90,000 pull requests to 2,294 benchmark tasks.
We begin with repository selection. The dataset is derived from 12 popular open-source Python repositories, with emphasis on projects that are actively maintained, follow clearer contribution practices, and provide stronger test coverage. Each pull request is anchored to a base commit, which defines the exact pre-fix repository snapshot used later in evaluation. This stage establishes the realism of the benchmark at the repository level. Every task originates from an actual codebase, an actual development history, and a concrete issue-resolution workflow.
The second stage applies attribute-based filtering. A pull request is retained only if it resolves a GitHub issue and modifies test files. The first condition provides the natural-language problem statement, since the issue text becomes the model input. The second condition introduces an initial signal that the pull request encodes intended behavior through tests rather than through an unverified code edit alone.
In effect, this stage aligns three objects: an issue description, a code change, and a test change. That alignment is essential. Without it, the benchmark would contain many maintenance edits or refactors that do not represent meaningful software engineering tasks.
The final stage is execution-based filtering. For each candidate task, the benchmark first applies the pull request’s test content to the base commit and records the test outcomes before the solution patch is introduced. It then applies the remaining pull request content and records the outcomes again. A task is retained only if at least one test exhibits a fail-to-pass transition after the solution patch is applied. Instances that trigger installation or runtime errors are removed as well.
This criterion is the key to non-triviality. A fail-to-pass test shows that the issue corresponds to a real behavioral defect, that the added or modified tests expose the defect in the pre-fix code, and that the reference patch changes execution in a way that resolves it. The paper further notes that every SWE-bench instance contains at least one fail-to-pass test, and a substantial fraction contain more than one, which strengthens the robustness of evaluation.
The three stages enforce three distinct properties. The first stage ensures realistic source material. The second ensures semantic grounding between issue text and code change. The third ensures behavioral validity under execution. This design is what separates SWE-bench from function-level code benchmarks. The benchmark does not ask whether a model can produce plausible code in isolation. It asks whether a model can interpret a real issue, modify a real repository, and generate a patch that survives repository tests.

title: Agentic AI Series: SWE-bench
text:
3 Autonomous Coding Agents
SWE-bench has had a significant influence on the development of autonomous coding systems because it reframes software engineering as a repository-level issue resolution task. Rather than evaluating isolated code generation, the benchmark evaluates whether a system can interpret an issue, navigate a repository, produce a patch, and verify the fix through test execution. This formulation naturally aligns with the design of autonomous coding agents that operate through iterative interaction with a codebase.
The benchmark therefore provides a realistic evaluation environment for systems that combine reasoning, retrieval, code editing, and execution.

3.1 SWE-agent
One direct connection is the emergence of SWE-agent–style systems (Yang et al. 2024). These systems treat software engineering as a sequential decision-making process in which the model interacts with a repository through a series of actions. Typical actions include searching the codebase, inspecting files, generating patches, and running tests.
The task structure used in SWE-bench closely matches this workflow. Each benchmark instance begins with an issue description and a repository snapshot, and success is determined by whether a generated patch resolves the issue according to the repository’s tests. This setup allows agent-based systems to be evaluated under realistic conditions, where solving the task requires exploration of the repository and iterative refinement of candidate fixes.
As a result, SWE-bench provides a natural testing ground for agentic approaches that combine language models with tools for code navigation and execution.


3.2 Autonomous Coding Systems
SWE-bench also motivated the development of more general autonomous coding systems that aim to automate repository maintenance tasks. These systems extend beyond single-shot code generation by incorporating multiple components such as retrieval modules, code editing mechanisms, and execution feedback loops.
Within the SWE-bench framework, these components correspond to different stages of the issue-resolution process. Retrieval mechanisms help identify relevant files within large repositories. Code generation modules propose candidate patches. Execution feedback from the test suite provides an objective signal indicating whether the proposed fix is successful.
The benchmark highlights the need for systems that integrate these capabilities rather than relying solely on direct text generation.


3.3 Agentic Software Engineering Workflows
More broadly, SWE-bench supports the evaluation of agentic software engineering workflows. In these workflows, the language model acts as a coordinator that plans and executes a sequence of operations required to resolve an issue. These operations may include reading documentation, examining source files, generating edits, and validating changes through test execution.
The benchmark is particularly useful for this line of research because it defines success behaviorally. A solution is considered correct only if the generated patch resolves the issue according to the repository’s tests. This allows different system architectures—such as retrieval-based pipelines, long-context models, and decision-making agents—to be compared under a common evaluation setting.
The importance of SWE-bench lies in how it shifts the focus of evaluation. Instead of measuring the ability to generate short code snippets, the benchmark evaluates the ability to complete a realistic software engineering task from start to finish. This requires identifying relevant context, proposing code modifications, and validating those modifications through execution.
For this reason, SWE-bench has become a useful benchmark for research on autonomous coding agents. It provides a standardized environment in which systems designed for repository-level reasoning and automated issue resolution can be tested and compared.

title: Agentic AI Series: SWE-bench
text:
4 Context Length and Retrieval
The SWE-bench evaluation reveals an important empirical pattern: model performance often decreases as the amount of provided repository context increases. Although one might expect larger context windows or broader retrieval to improve performance, the experiments show that providing more files or longer contexts can reduce task success for the evaluated models.
This observation highlights a central challenge in repository-level software engineering. The relevant implementation details required to resolve an issue typically occupy only a small portion of the repository, and increasing the amount of visible code does not necessarily improve the model’s ability to identify and modify the correct location.

4.1 Context Length
The paper reports a negative correlation between context length and model performance. As the total input context increases, the success rate of evaluated models decreases. This behavior is particularly visible for Claude 2 and is also observed for other models in the benchmark.
In the experiments, models often achieve their best performance under shorter context limits. Increasing the amount of code provided to the model does not consistently improve results, suggesting that simply expanding the available context does not resolve the underlying difficulty of repository-level reasoning.
The paper also investigates retrieval-based approaches using BM25 to select repository files that may be relevant to the issue description. Increasing the number of retrieved files improves the recall of files that were actually modified in the human-written fix, sometimes referred to as oracle files.
However, despite improving oracle recall, the overall task success rate decreases as more files are retrieved. This indicates that improved retrieval recall does not necessarily translate into improved patch generation performance.
One factor contributing to this behavior is the presence of irrelevant code in the expanded context. When additional files are retrieved, the model must process many pieces of code that are unrelated to the issue being resolved. Under these conditions, the model may struggle to identify the specific code region that requires modification.
The benchmark therefore highlights a limitation in the ability of current models to localize the problematic code within a large repository context. The paper notes that these results are consistent with prior work suggesting that language models can struggle when relevant information appears deep within long contexts. When many files are included in the input, the code segments that contain the actual defect may become harder for the model to identify. This observation further illustrates the difficulty of reasoning over long and heterogeneous repository contexts.


4.2 Distribution Shift
The paper also reports a related issue for fine-tuned models such as SWE-Llama. During training, SWE-Llama is provided with oracle files corresponding exactly to the files modified in the reference solution. As a result, the model learns a setting in which each provided file is likely to require modification.
At inference time, however, BM25 retrieval introduces additional files that are not intended to be edited. This creates a distribution shift between the training configuration and the inference environment. When the model encounters these additional files, it may attempt to edit code that should remain unchanged, which can further reduce performance.
These findings suggest that repository-level software engineering requires more than simply increasing the amount of context available to a model. Effective systems must also be able to identify the small subset of repository files that are relevant to a given issue and focus modification efforts on those locations. SWE-bench therefore highlights the importance of context selection, code localization, and repository-scale reasoning in LLM-based software engineering systems.

title: Agentic AI Series: SWE-bench
text:
5 Research Implications
SWE-bench highlights a shift in emphasis for LLM-based software engineering. The benchmark is not primarily about isolated function completion. Instead, it evaluates whether a model can resolve a real GitHub issue in a real repository by generating a patch that passes the relevant tests. In this setting, several research challenges become especially visible.

5.1 Repository-Scale Code Understanding
A central challenge is repository-scale code understanding. SWE-bench tasks are defined over full repository snapshots rather than small, self-contained programs. The paper emphasizes that the relevant edits are typically a small subset of the overall codebase, which means the model must operate in an environment where most available code is irrelevant to the immediate fix. This makes repository-scale understanding a central requirement of the benchmark.
This difficulty is reflected in the scale of the data. The paper reports that the average repository contains thousands of non-test files and hundreds of thousands of lines of code. Under these conditions, solving the task is not simply a matter of continuing a local code pattern. It requires identifying the parts of the repository that are most relevant to the issue.


5.2 Long-Context Reasoning
SWE-bench also highlights the challenge of long-context reasoning. The paper notes that the repository context is far larger than the context window of most language models evaluated in the study. As a result, the full codebase cannot be provided directly to the model. This makes context selection and representation an important part of the problem setting.
The paper therefore motivates approaches that can work under limited context budgets, including retrieval-based methods and long-context models. The benchmark is useful precisely because it exposes the gap between the size of real repositories and the amount of code a model can inspect at once.


5.3 Edit Localization
Another challenge made visible by SWE-bench is the problem of identifying where edits are needed. The paper does not frame this as a separate formal task, but it repeatedly emphasizes that successful solutions require finding the relatively small number of lines that must be modified within a much larger repository. It also notes that even oracle retrieval is unrealistic in practice, since one typically does not know in advance which files will need to change.
For this reason, the benchmark makes clear that repository-level software engineering is not only a generation problem. It is also a problem of locating the relevant implementation context from a natural-language issue description.


5.4 Multi-File Patch Generation
SWE-bench further highlights the challenge of multi-file patch generation. The paper reports that reference solutions often require edits across multiple files and functions rather than a single local change. This means that the benchmark tests whether a model can produce repository-consistent modifications rather than only isolated code completions.
This aspect of the benchmark is important because it more closely resembles practical software maintenance. A correct patch may involve changes to core logic, helper functions, and associated tests, all of which must remain consistent under execution.

title: Agentic AI Series: SWE-bench
text:
6 Conclusion
Taken together, these challenges explain why SWE-bench is a useful benchmark for LLM-based software engineering. It highlights difficulties that are largely hidden by function-level benchmarks: operating over large repositories, working under limited context windows, identifying the relevant edit locations, and generating patches that may span multiple files. The paper presents SWE-bench as a setting that can be used to compare retrieval methods, long-context models, and decision-making agents on more realistic software engineering tasks.
In this sense, SWE-bench does not simply make coding tasks harder. It makes the evaluation setting closer to real software engineering by shifting the focus from local code synthesis to repository-level issue resolution.

title: On-Policy Distillation: The Two Knobs Hidden Inside Knowledge Distillation
text:
2026-05-24
Distilling a small autoregressive model from a big one had been treated as a regression problem: collect a dataset, have the teacher label it, train the student to match. GKD recasts that setup as imitation learning with an interactive expert (Agarwal et al. 2023). The teacher isn’t a fixed answer key; it’s an expert you can query on whatever states the student wanders into. Once that relabeling lands, a prescription follows almost mechanically — train the student on the sequences the student itself generates, and ask the teacher to grade them token by token — and the vague complaint about “distribution mismatch” sharpens into a named, well-studied phenomenon: covariate shift.
That reframing does something structural: it reveals that “knowledge distillation,” as practiced, had quietly bundled two independent choices into one. The first is which sequences the student trains on — a fixed dataset, the teacher’s samples, or the student’s own outputs. The second is which divergence measures the gap between student and teacher at each token — forward KL, reverse KL, or something between. GKD pulls these apart into two knobs, a data fraction and a divergence, and a large part of the paper is simply a careful study of what each knob does on its own. Reading it this way, the experiments stop looking like a leaderboard and start looking like a map: this knob fixes the train/inference gap and behaves consistently across tasks; that knob trades quality against diversity and only matters once you decode by sampling.

title: On-Policy Distillation: The Two Knobs Hidden Inside Knowledge Distillation
section: 1 The Covariate Shift That Supervised Distillation Walks Into
text:
1 The Covariate Shift That Supervised Distillation Walks Into
Start with the failure the method is built to fix, because it is sharper than “the training and test distributions differ.” Supervised distillation trains the student to match the teacher on a fixed set of sequences — either ground-truth targets or sequences the teacher generated. In imitation-learning terms that is behavioral cloning: the student learns the expert’s action (the teacher’s next-token distribution) on states drawn from the expert’s trajectory, never on the states the student will produce when it runs on its own.
For an autoregressive model that gap compounds. Every token the student emits becomes part of the context conditioning the next token. Make one off-distribution choice and the prefix y_{<n} is now something the training data never showed — so the next prediction is worse, which corrupts the prefix further, and the error cascades down the sequence. This is exposure bias, and the imitation-learning literature has both a name for its cause and a recipe for its cure: the cause is covariate shift, and the cure is to collect data under the learner’s own policy and have the expert relabel it. That recipe is the on-policy imitation approach the paper draws on; on-policy KD applies it with the teacher’s full token distribution standing in for the expert’s correction.
What the interactive expert provides over a frozen teacher-generated dataset is precision about where the correction lands. A static dataset of teacher samples corrects the student on states the teacher visits. An interactive teacher corrects the student on the states the student visits — exactly the off-distribution prefixes that drive the cascade. That difference is what makes “interactive expert” more than a vocabulary upgrade: it changes which data the gradient sees.

title: On-Policy Distillation: The Two Knobs Hidden Inside Knowledge Distillation
section: 2 Why On-Policy Data Didn’t Need Reinforcement-Learning Machinery
text:
2 Why On-Policy Data Didn’t Need Reinforcement-Learning Machinery
On-policy imitation was standard in robotics and RL well before this paper, which raises a natural question: why hadn’t it been pointed at language-model distillation? Part of the answer is a reasonable-looking assumption — that learning on self-generated sequences requires RL machinery, with sampling inside the objective, gradients pushed back through a stochastic policy, and the variance and instability that come with it.
Two pieces make the simpler regime possible, and the first is what the teacher provides as a label. The per-sequence divergence GKD minimizes is a length-normalized average of per-token divergences:

\mathcal{D}\big(p_T \,\|\, p_S^\theta\big)(y|x) := \frac{1}{L_y} \sum_{n=1}^{L_y} \mathcal{D}\big(p_T(\cdot|y_{<n},x) \,\|\, p_S^\theta(\cdot|y_{<n}, x)\big)

At every one of the L_y positions the label is the teacher’s entire next-token distribution over the vocabulary, not a single sampled token and not a scalar reward arriving only at the end of the sequence. That density is the lever. RL on language models is hard in large part because the reward is sparse and scalar, which forces high-variance credit assignment back across the whole generation; here the teacher delivers a full supervised target at each step, so there is nothing sparse to propagate.
The second piece is the on-policy loss itself, which shows why the RL machinery can be set aside:

L_{OD}(\theta) := \mathbb{E}_{x \sim X} \Big[\,\mathbb{E}_{y \sim p_S(\cdot|x)} \big[\,\mathcal{D}_{KL}\big(p_T \,\|\, p_S^\theta\big)(y|x)\big] \Big]

The form matters, so it’s worth tracing where the gradient actually goes. The student samples a sequence y from its own current distribution p_S(\cdot|x), but the method does not differentiate through that sampling step — the sampled sequence is frozen and treated as data, and only the inner divergence between teacher and student token distributions is differentiated. That single choice keeps the update structurally identical to ordinary supervised distillation; the only thing that changed is which sequences populate the batch. Because the teacher hands over a dense per-token distribution as the label, there is no scalar reward and no policy-gradient estimator to stabilize. The reason this is written with a stop-gradient rather than as full sequence-level optimization is precisely to stay in supervised-training territory while still training on on-policy data.
That same stop-gradient is what separates GKD from the concurrent MiniLLM, which frames distillation as RL and does backpropagate through sampling via policy gradient — and consequently needs a set of stabilizers for high variance, reward hacking, and generation-length bias. GKD trades that machinery for the simpler regime, at the cost of one honest subtlety the source’s own author comments flag: with the stop-gradient in place, the objective being minimized is not the sequence-level divergence (the sampling distribution that the gradient ignores does depend on \theta). What is minimized is the teacher–student token divergence averaged over the student’s current output distribution, treated as data and refreshed each step. It is a moving target optimized as if it were stationary within a step — a pragmatic relaxation that the results bear out, but not the same object the name might suggest.

title: On-Policy Distillation: The Two Knobs Hidden Inside Knowledge Distillation
text:
3 One Objective, Two Knobs
The generalization that gives the paper its name writes both design choices into a single line:

L_\mathrm{GKD}(\theta) := (1 - \lambda)\, \mathbb{E}_{(x, y) \sim (X, Y)} \big[\, \mathcal{D}(p_T \| p_S^\theta)(y|x) \big] + \lambda\, \mathbb{E}_{x\sim X} \Big[\,\mathbb{E}_{y \sim p_S(\cdot|x)} \big[\,\mathcal{D}(p_T \| p_S^\theta)(y|x)\big]\Big]

The point of writing it this way is that the two terms are the same divergence evaluated on two different data sources — fixed sequences on the left, student-generated sequences on the right — mixed by \lambda, while the divergence \mathcal{D} is a free choice applied identically to both. That makes the data axis (\lambda) and the loss axis (\mathcal{D}) genuinely independent. Supervised KD is (\lambda{=}0, \text{forward KL}). On-policy KD is (\lambda{=}1, \text{forward KL}). ImitKD turns out to be forward KL with a \lambda schedule sitting around the middle; f-distill is mixed data with total-variation distance. Every prior method is a single point in this plane, and each had fixed one axis while varying the other.
Separating the axes is what lets the experiments say something the prior framing could not: that the two knobs carry different kinds of information. The rest of the paper is, in effect, turning each knob with the other held fixed and reporting what moves.

3.1 What the Data Knob Controls
Across summarization (XSum), translation (WMT en→de), and grade-school math (GSM8K), and across student sizes from 77M to 800M against a ~3B T5-XL teacher, the consistent pattern is that raising \lambda toward 1 helps. Purely on-policy and mixed variants outperform the supervised-only variants regardless of which divergence is used. Averaged across student sizes, on-policy GKD’s improvement over the starting student is roughly 2.1\times the improvement that baseline KD methods achieve on summarization, 1.7\times on translation, and 1.9\times on reasoning. The data knob behaves consistently from task to task in a way the divergence knob does not.
Two of the data-knob results are worth reading precisely, because their headline phrasing can carry more than the experiment establishes. The most quotable is that a T5 model roughly 7000\times smaller than PaLM-540B surpasses PaLM’s few-shot performance on XSum. What that comparison establishes is narrow: XSum is a specific abstractive-summarization target, and a small model fine-tuned and then distilled on it can beat a much larger model that gets zero task adaptation, because the comparison sets specialization against few-shot generalization. It speaks to the value of task-specific distillation in general; the GKD-specific evidence is the like-for-like comparison, on-policy GKD against supervised KD, SeqKD, ImitKD, and f-distill at the same student size and teacher.
The data-efficiency result is the sharper one. On-policy GKD trained on 5% of XSum, using no ground-truth summaries, outperforms supervised KD and ImitKD trained on the full dataset with ground truth. The mechanism behind it is specific: on-policy KD needs only input prompts, because the teacher supplies the labels on the student’s own outputs, so the comparison is really teacher token-level supervision on on-policy states against ground-truth supervision on off-policy states. The result shows the former carries more signal here — which is a statement about where supervision should be applied, and one that leans on the teacher being strong enough for its per-token distributions to be a richer target than a single reference summary.
GSM8K adds a detail more informative than it first appears: performance improves with the on-policy fraction only once at least a quarter of the data is student-generated. A threshold rather than a smooth ramp is itself a clue about the mechanism. Covariate-shift correction is a distributional effect — it engages only when the student’s own states make up enough of the batch to shift the training distribution. A small trickle of on-policy samples diluted in a mostly-fixed dataset doesn’t move the distribution the gradient sees, so the student remains effectively behaviorally cloned; past the threshold, the student’s own state distribution starts to define what gets trained on, and the corrective loop takes hold.


3.2 What the Divergence Knob Controls
The divergence choice looks task-dependent and a little mysterious until it is lined up against the decoding strategy, at which point it resolves into a single mechanism.
That mechanism is capacity mismatch. A small student cannot exactly reproduce a 3B teacher’s token distribution, so the only question is how to be wrong, and the two KLs answer it differently because they are asymmetric in opposite directions. Forward KL, \sum_c p_T(c)\log\frac{p_T(c)}{p_S(c)}, is weighted by the teacher: wherever the teacher places mass, the student is heavily penalized for placing little, so a low-capacity student spreads its limited budget to cover the teacher’s whole support — mode-covering, which means smearing probability onto tokens the teacher itself finds unlikely. Reverse KL swaps the roles: weighted by the student, it punishes the student for putting mass where the teacher has little, so the student retreats onto the teacher’s high-probability tokens and abandons the rest — mode-seeking, which buys per-token quality at the cost of diversity.
Whether that difference is ever felt depends on how you decode. Under temperature sampling you draw from the spread-out tail, so a mode-covering student periodically emits the low-quality tokens it smeared mass onto, and quality drops — mode-seeking divergences (reverse KL, JSD(0.9)) pull ahead. Under greedy decoding you only ever emit the argmax, the badly-allocated tail is never sampled, and the choice of divergence barely affects performance. The interaction is not task magic: the divergence shapes the tail of the distribution, and only sampling-based decoding visits the tail.
This is also the clearest reason the paper bothers with the generalized Jensen–Shannon divergence rather than only offering the two KLs:

\mathcal{D}_{JSD(\beta)}(P\|Q) = \beta\,\mathcal{D}_{KL}\big(P \,\|\, \beta P + (1-\beta)Q\big) + (1-\beta)\,\mathcal{D}_{KL}\big(Q \,\|\, \beta P + (1-\beta)Q\big)

Why this form? The paper notes that JSD(\beta) behaves like forward KL as \beta\to0 and like reverse KL as \beta\to1, so the endpoints just recover the two KLs and the value of JSD has to live in its interior. And it does: JSD(0.9) is mostly mode-seeking but still penalized for dropping teacher mass entirely, a blend the two endpoints cannot express. It captures much of reverse KL’s quality benefit under sampling without fully abandoning coverage, and unlike raw KL it stays finite even when student and teacher supports disagree — the disjoint-support situation a weak student tends to create. The interior is useful exactly when the right amount of mode-seeking is somewhere short of “all.”

title: On-Policy Distillation: The Two Knobs Hidden Inside Knowledge Distillation
section: 4 Swapping the Regularizer in RL Fine-Tuning
text:
4 Swapping the Regularizer in RL Fine-Tuning
The contribution that is easy to skim past is what happens when on-policy distillation is folded into RL fine-tuning. Because GKD needs only student samples, it drops into an RLHF-style loop:

\mathbb{E}_{x\sim X} \Big[(1-\alpha)\, \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{y \sim p_S^\theta(\cdot|x)} \left[r(y)\right]}_{\text{RL objective}} - \alpha \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{y \sim p_S(\cdot|x)} \big[\mathcal{D}(p_T \| p_S^\theta)(y|x)\big]}_{\text{On-policy distillation}} \Big]

The structurally interesting part is what the second term regularizes toward. Standard RLHF maximizes reward minus a KL penalty that keeps the model close to its initial supervised checkpoint (Ouyang et al. 2022); that penalty is conservative — it can keep the model from drifting, but it cannot add capability. Replacing the anchor with the teacher policy changes the character of the penalty: regularizing toward a stronger model pulls the policy toward a better distribution while the reward term chases the metric. The paper’s related work flags this as “quite different from an optimization perspective” despite looking natural, and the distinction is real — the regularizer has gone from “stay put” to “move toward something better.”
The motivating target is the alignment tax, the capability erosion RLHF tends to introduce. The XSum experiment is where this is exercised: combining a textual-entailment reward (to suppress hallucination) with on-policy GKD, the model exceeds a self-regularized RLHF baseline on summarization quality and surpasses the teacher on factual consistency. The setup recovers some of both capability and reward rather than trading one for the other, which is the concrete sense in which the regularizer swap is meant to help.

title: On-Policy Distillation: The Two Knobs Hidden Inside Knowledge Distillation
section: 5 Two Things the Paper Leaves Open
text:
5 Two Things the Paper Leaves Open
A neutral reading of the method surfaces two questions the paper does not fully settle, and both are worth stating plainly rather than resolving past the evidence.
The first is whether “on-policy” is the operative mechanism or a description of something simpler. GKD’s procedure — generate samples from the student, whose quality rises as the student improves, and train on them with teacher labels — sits close to iterated self-training. ReST and the self-play methods also generate their own data and train on the good parts, differing mainly in whether the filter is “match the teacher” or “clear a reward threshold” (Gulcehre et al. 2023; Chen et al. 2024). So two explanations fit the same curves: covariate-shift correction in the imitation-learning sense, and the plainer story that the student simply gets more and fresher self-relevant training signal. The experiment that would separate them — holding the data distribution fixed while toggling whether labels come from the teacher’s full distribution versus a hard self-label, and whether on-policy samples are refreshed or frozen — is not run. The self-distillation result narrows the space: with student and teacher sharing architecture and size, so no capacity gap, on-policy GKD still beats supervised KD and the self-distilled student surpasses its teacher. That rules out “the teacher is simply better and on-policy data is incidental,” since the gain appears with no capacity gap at all. It does not, on its own, distinguish the covariate-shift account from the fresh-data account, because both predict that outcome. The honest summary is that on-policy data clearly does real work — the monotone \lambda sweeps and the self-distillation result are not artifacts — while the precise mechanism remains an open question the paper’s evidence is consistent with but does not pin down.
The second open question is cost, which the paper treats briefly. Student sampling adds roughly 1.8\times to 2.2\times overhead on GSM8K, and the overhead grows as the student gets larger relative to the teacher — 1.8\times at a 38\times size gap (T5-small), rising to 2.2\times at a 3.8\times gap (T5-large). The defense offered is a single sentence: if sampling from the student during fine-tuning is too costly, serving that student to users would be too costly as well. That argument compares two cost regimes that behave differently. Serving cost is amortized over a large request volume — the reason to want a small student in the first place — while training cost is paid up front across tens of thousands of steps, each requiring full autoregressive generation (the slow part of inference) plus a teacher forward pass, with no amortization. The two are not interchangeable, and the relationship between them depends on request volume, number of training steps, and student size in ways the one-sentence treatment doesn’t develop. The appendix’s quieter framing is the more load-bearing one: the overhead is under 2.2\times and may be worth the quality gain, and it nearly vanishes when GKD is combined with RL fine-tuning, since the RL loop already generates from the student and GKD then adds only a teacher inference pass for logits. When on-policy distillation is cheap and when it is not is a practical question the paper opens more than it closes.
Holding those two open questions alongside the rest leaves a coherent picture. The reframing of distillation as imitation learning is the move that organizes everything; from it follows the prescription to train on the student’s own outputs, the clean factoring into a data knob and a divergence knob, and a usable rule for setting them — push \lambda toward 1, then choose the divergence by whether the deployed model will sample or greedy-decode. What that rule does to the underlying distribution, and what it costs to apply, are the threads the paper hands forward.

title: AI Agent Design Patterns: From Intent to Execution
AI Agent Design Patterns: From Intent to Execution
text:
1 Problem Setup
Modern agent systems are often described through an oversimplified abstraction. A common formulation assumes that one provides a model with a prompt, exposes a set of tools, and allows the model to act. While this description is sufficient for small-scale demonstrations, it becomes inadequate once the system supports delegation, background execution, isolated environments, or long-running tasks.
In such settings, the primary challenge is no longer prompt design. The central problem becomes routing.
Routing refers to the layer that determines the computational interpretation of a request. Given a high-level instruction, the system must decide where the work executes, how it is scheduled, how it is tracked, and which runtime object represents it. The purpose of this discussion is to formalize this layer as a mapping from model intent to an explicit task contract.

title: AI Agent Design Patterns: From Intent to Execution
text:
2 From Prompting to Systems Design
Consider a coordinator agent that produces high-level instructions such as parallel research, isolated implementation, continuation of an existing worker, or background verification. These outputs reflect meaningful decisions at the level of intent.
However, these decisions are not yet executable. A concrete system must still resolve execution semantics, including whether the work runs in the foreground or background, whether execution occurs locally or remotely, whether a new worker is instantiated or an existing one is resumed, and how lifecycle events such as cancellation or monitoring are handled.
This motivates a strict separation between intent and execution semantics. The model specifies what should be done, while the runtime determines how it is realized. Maintaining this boundary is a key principle in stable agent architectures.

title: AI Agent Design Patterns: From Intent to Execution
text:
3 Three-Layer Architecture
A structured design separates the system into three layers: the policy layer, the routing layer, and the task contract layer. Each layer corresponds to a distinct abstraction boundary.

3.1 Policy Layer
The policy layer defines the decision surface of the model. It specifies the coordinator role, the available tools, the capabilities of workers, and the general orchestration rules. This layer shapes behavior indirectly by influencing the distribution over actions.
Formally, one may view the policy as a mapping 
\pi_\theta(a \mid s),
 where s encodes the current context and a represents a high-level delegation action.
The policy layer should remain lightweight. Its purpose is to guide decision-making rather than instantiate runtime objects.


3.2 Routing Layer
The routing layer transforms high-level actions into execution paths. Given a delegation request, the router selects a task kind based on constraints such as isolation requirements or execution mode.
This can be formalized as a deterministic mapping 
k = f_{\text{route}}(r),
 where r denotes the request and k denotes the selected execution type.
At this stage, abstract intent is converted into a concrete execution structure.


3.3 Task Contract Layer
Once a route is selected, the system constructs a task contract. This object represents the work explicitly and defines its lifecycle, identity, status, and outputs.
The task contract ensures that execution is observable and controllable. It provides a structured interface for monitoring progress, handling cancellation, and managing persistence.

title: AI Agent Design Patterns: From Intent to Execution
section: 4 Why Policy Should Not Create Tasks
text:
4 Why Policy Should Not Create Tasks
A common design error is to allow the policy layer to instantiate tasks directly. This blurs the boundary between soft decision logic and hard execution semantics.
The distinction matters because prompt-based logic is inherently unstable. It changes as role descriptions, tool definitions, and orchestration heuristics are revised. Execution semantics, by contrast, should remain deterministic. Decisions such as whether work runs in the background, whether isolation is required, how lifecycle transitions are handled, and how outputs are persisted must be governed by code rather than prompt wording.
Once these concerns are mixed, both layers become harder to maintain. Small prompt edits can unintentionally alter runtime behavior, while execution rules become difficult to reason about and enforce. For this reason, policy should shape routing decisions, but it should not replace routing logic.
This separation also clarifies the role of the agent builder. In practice, the builder is not merely a construction utility. It validates requests, resolves constraints, selects execution modes, assembles runtime parameters, and creates task contracts. Architecturally, it is best understood as a combination of a router and a factory, operating at the boundary between model-generated intent and system-level execution.

title: AI Agent Design Patterns: From Intent to Execution
text:
5 Task Contracts
The task contract is a central abstraction in multi-agent systems. Without it, execution remains implicit and difficult to control. With it, work becomes a first-class object that can be inspected, stored, and managed.
A well-defined task contract answers several questions: the type of the task, its current state, its output location, and whether it can be resumed or terminated. This explicit representation distinguishes robust runtimes from ad hoc orchestration systems.
The following example illustrates a minimal contract structure.
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from enum import Enum
from typing import Optional
import time
import uuid


class TaskStatus(str, Enum):
    PENDING = "pending"
    RUNNING = "running"
    COMPLETED = "completed"
    FAILED = "failed"
    KILLED = "killed"


class TaskKind(str, Enum):
    LOCAL_FOREGROUND = "local_foreground"
    LOCAL_BACKGROUND = "local_background"
    REMOTE = "remote"
    TEAMMATE = "teammate"


@dataclass
class Task:
    id: str
    kind: TaskKind
    status: TaskStatus
    description: str
    prompt: str
    output_path: str
    start_time: float
    end_time: Optional[float] = None
    notified: bool = False


def create_task(kind: TaskKind, description: str, prompt: str) -> Task:
    task_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
    return Task(
        id=task_id,
        kind=kind,
        status=TaskStatus.PENDING,
        description=description,
        prompt=prompt,
        output_path=f"/tmp/tasks/{task_id}.log",
        start_time=time.time(),
    )
Although the exact fields may vary, the key idea is that execution is represented explicitly rather than embedded in prompt flow.
