A reward model that ranks candidate solutions is only as reliable as the labels it was trained on. For multi-step mathematical reasoning there are two ways to supply those labels. Outcome supervision provides a single label per solution, derived from whether the final answer is correct. Process supervision provides a label for each intermediate step. The paper compares the reward models these two regimes produce, on solutions to problems from the MATH dataset, and finds that process supervision yields the stronger model (Lightman et al. 2023). The best process-supervised reward model selects a correct solution for 78.2\% of a representative MATH test subset under best-of-1860 search, against 72.4\% for the outcome-supervised baseline and 69.6\% for majority voting.
The comparison matters because a single logical error is enough to invalidate a long derivation, and a reward model used for search must detect such errors. Earlier work compared the two supervision regimes on grade-school math and found similar final-answer accuracy, with process supervision reaching it using less data (Cobbe et al. 2021). This paper changes three variables — a more capable base model, substantially more human feedback, and the harder MATH dataset — and reaches a separation between the regimes rather than parity. Alongside the result it releases PRM800K, the full set of 800,000 step-level human labels used to train the best reward model.

title: LLM Reasoning Series: Process Supervision and Step-Level Reward Models
section: 1 Two Reward Models, Two Label Sources
text:
1 Two Reward Models, Two Label Sources
The object of study is the reward model, not the generator. A single fixed model, the generator, produces all candidate solutions in a newline-delimited step-by-step format; it is not trained with reinforcement learning. Both reward models are trained on solutions from this generator and differ only in the labels they receive.
The outcome-supervised reward model (ORM) is trained as in the token-level verifiers of the predecessor work (Cobbe et al. 2021). The training set is a fixed number of uniformly sampled solutions per problem — 100 at large scale — each labeled correct or incorrect by automatically checking the final answer. The model predicts this label at every token; the prediction at the final token is taken as the solution score at test time. The automatic grading is the source of the regime’s central weakness: a solution that reaches the correct answer through incorrect reasoning is labeled correct, a false positive the ORM cannot distinguish from a genuinely correct solution.
The process-supervised reward model (PRM) is trained on per-step labels collected from human data-labelers, who mark each step positive, negative, or neutral. A positive step is correct and advances the solution; a negative step is incorrect or unreasonable; a neutral step is ambiguous — correct but subtly misleading, or a valid but poor suggestion. The neutral category exists to defer a decision: at test time a neutral label can be treated as either positive or negative, and the choice is made empirically rather than during annotation. The PRM is trained to predict these labels by maximizing the log-likelihood of the target label token after the last token of each step, which keeps training inside a standard language-model pipeline with no special machinery.
Process supervision is provided only up to the first incorrect step. This is a deliberate design choice, and the reason is that it makes the comparison between the regimes fair rather than favorable to process supervision. On a correct solution both regimes convey the same information: every step is correct. On an incorrect solution both reveal that at least one error exists, and process supervision additionally reveals where the first error is — but no further. Supervising past the first error would widen the information gap and also raise the human labeling cost, because without a checkable final answer, judging a full solution’s correctness reduces to finding its first mistake. Stopping at the first error holds the labeling cost of the two regimes approximately equal, so the comparison isolates the value of step-level location, not the value of more labels.

title: LLM Reasoning Series: Process Supervision and Step-Level Reward Models
section: 2 Scoring a Solution from Step Probabilities
text:
2 Scoring a Solution from Step Probabilities
A reward model used for best-of-N search must reduce a solution to one comparable score. For the ORM this is the final-token prediction. For the PRM, which emits a correctness probability p_i for each of the K steps, the per-step scores must be combined. The paper defines the solution score as the probability that every step is correct, implemented as the product of the step probabilities:

s(\text{solution}) \;=\; \prod_{i=1}^{K} p_i .

Why the product? The product is the joint probability that all steps are correct when the step events are treated as independent. This matches the quantity a verifier should report for search: a solution is useful only if it is correct from start to finish, so its score should fall as soon as any step is doubtful. The natural alternative is the minimum, \min_i p_i, which scores a solution by its single weakest step. The paper evaluates both reductions, crossed with the two readings of the neutral label, and reports best-of-1860 test accuracy of 78.2\% for product with neutrals counted positive, 77.6\% for minimum with neutrals positive, 77.4\% and 77.8\% for the two negative-neutral variants. The differences are small; product with neutral-as-positive is selected.
The product reduction carries a structural property the paper notes explicitly: because every factor is at most one, appending more steps can only lower the score, so the product is slightly biased against solutions with more steps. The minimum does not share this bias, since it depends on a single step regardless of length. The near-equal accuracies indicate that this length bias does not materially affect ranking on MATH, but it is the kind of artifact that becomes relevant when solutions vary widely in step count.

title: LLM Reasoning Series: Process Supervision and Step-Level Reward Models
section: 3 Best-of-N as the Measure of Reliability
text:
3 Best-of-N as the Measure of Reliability
A reward model is evaluated by best-of-N search over uniform samples from the generator. For each test problem the N sampled solutions are scored, the highest-scoring one is selected, and it is graded by its final answer:

\hat{y} \;=\; \arg\max_{i \in \{1,\dots,N\}} s\big(x,\, y_i\big).

The fraction of problems for which \hat{y} is correct is the reported metric. This metric is chosen over training the generator with reinforcement learning because it isolates the reward model: the generator is fixed, so any difference in the reported accuracy is attributable to the reward model’s ability to rank a correct solution above its competitors. A model that ranks correct solutions highest more often is the more reliable one, by definition of the task.
At large scale the PRM exceeds both the ORM and the majority-voting baseline at every value of N, and the gap widens as N grows. The widening is the informative part. Majority voting aggregates final answers and is a strong baseline because a correct answer is often the plurality, but it ignores the reasoning entirely. As N increases the sample set contains more convincing wrong-answer solutions, and a reward model that scores by surface plausibility will increasingly select them. That the PRM’s lead grows with N indicates it continues to separate correct from incorrect reasoning as the pool of distractors expands, where the ORM and majority voting do not.

title: LLM Reasoning Series: Process Supervision and Step-Level Reward Models
section: 4 Isolating the Comparison with Synthetic Supervision
text:
4 Isolating the Comparison with Synthetic Supervision
The large-scale result is confounded. The PRM and ORM training sets are not comparable: the PRM set was built with active learning, is biased toward wrong-answer solutions, and is an order of magnitude smaller, while the ORM set is 100 uniform samples per problem with no overlap. And the ORM’s final-answer grading admits false positives that may depress its performance — an effect one might or might not want to charge to outcome supervision as such. Collecting human labels to ablate these factors is too costly, so the paper substitutes a synthetic labeler: the large-scale PRM, denoted \text{PRM}_{\text{large}}, supervises a series of smaller reward models on identical datasets, with supervision form the only variable.
Three supervision signals are compared. Process supervision returns \text{PRM}_{\text{large}}’s step labels up to the first negative step, mimicking the human protocol. Outcome supervision from \text{PRM}_{\text{large}} marks a solution correct only if \text{PRM}_{\text{large}} judges every step correct. Outcome supervision from final-answer checking uses the automatic grader. Converting \text{PRM}_{\text{large}}’s probabilities into discrete step labels requires a threshold: a step is called incorrect when \text{PRM}_{\text{large}} assigns its negative label more than 20\% probability. The threshold is set below 50\% deliberately, because \text{PRM}_{\text{large}} is miscalibrated toward positive labels; a symmetric 50\% cut would inherit that bias and under-report errors, so the lower cut compensates for the known calibration skew.
With these controls, process supervision outperforms both outcome signals at every data-collection scale. Within the two outcome baselines, \text{PRM}_{\text{large}} supervision beats final-answer checking, because it supplies better labels to solutions that reach the correct answer through incorrect reasoning — exactly the false-positive case. The paper declines to declare one outcome baseline canonical: final-answer checking is more purely outcome-based, but its false-positive weakness is arguably over-represented on MATH, whereas \text{PRM}_{\text{large}} supervision better models outcome supervision in domains less prone to false positives. It treats the latter as the more relevant baseline while leaving the reader to weigh the choice. The comparison’s significance is that process supervision wins even when the outcome labels are made clean, which removes the false-positive explanation and isolates the advantage to step-level credit.

title: LLM Reasoning Series: Process Supervision and Step-Level Reward Models
section: 5 Active Learning and the Cost of Labels
text:
5 Active Learning and the Cost of Labels
Process supervision requires human labels, so its practical viability depends on label efficiency. The data-collection strategy surfaces the solutions most informative to label, which the paper operationalizes as convincing wrong-answer solutions: convincing meaning highly rated by the current best PRM, wrong-answer meaning the final answer is incorrect. Such a solution is known to contain at least one error the PRM has failed to catch, so labeling it is guaranteed to correct a model mistake, whereas a uniformly sampled solution is often correct or obviously wrong and teaches little.
The synthetic setup permits a controlled measurement. A small reward model \text{PRM}_{\text{selector}}, trained on one sample per problem, scores 1000 samples per problem; for each larger model, N samples per problem are selected so that 80\% are the most convincing wrong-answer samples under \text{PRM}_{\text{selector}} and 20\% are the most convincing remaining samples, correct or not. The 20\% admixture keeps the dataset from collapsing entirely onto wrong answers while preserving the property that most samples contain an error. Comparing the slope of accuracy against dataset size with and without this selection, active learning is approximately 2.6\times more data-efficient than uniform sampling.
The estimate has a documented boundary. The model trained on the largest active-learning dataset, 200 samples per problem, falls slightly below the trend, which the paper attributes to 200 being a large fraction of the 1000-sample selection pool, leaving too little diversity for selection to exploit. A preliminary attempt to retrain \text{PRM}_{\text{selector}} iteratively during collection produced instability the authors could not diagnose and no improvement, so the reported gain comes from a single fixed selector.

title: LLM Reasoning Series: Process Supervision and Step-Level Reward Models
section: 6 Generalization and the Source of the Advantage
text:
6 Generalization and the Source of the Advantage
To test whether the PRM’s advantage is specific to the MATH distribution, both large-scale models are evaluated on recent STEM exam questions — AP Calculus, AP Chemistry, AP Physics, and AMC10/12 — released after the pretraining corpus was assembled, so they cannot be contaminated. Across 234 problems in aggregate, best-of-100 selection gives the PRM 72.9\% against the ORM’s 63.8\% and majority voting’s 61.3\%, with the PRM ahead in every subject. The ordering observed on MATH holds on guaranteed-fresh problems, which both supports generalization and weakens the possibility that test-set contamination drives the main result.
The mechanism the paper offers for the advantage is credit assignment. An outcome-supervised model receiving a single negative label on a hard problem must infer which step was responsible, and on hard problems nearly every sampled solution contains an error, so the marginal information in one more negative outcome label is low. Process supervision states how many leading steps were correct and where the first error is, which is a denser signal and removes the inference. The paper presents this as the explanation for the performance gap, consistent with the synthetic result that the advantage survives after the false-positive confound is removed.
A second consequence concerns alignment. Safer training methods often reduce capability, a cost termed an alignment tax, and such a tax discourages adoption. Process supervision rewards a human-endorsed chain of reasoning directly rather than using the outcome as a proxy, which is more interpretable and less exposed to a model that learns to exploit an outcome proxy. Because process supervision is also the stronger method here, the paper characterizes its alignment tax as negative — the more interpretable signal is also the more accurate one — and argues this alignment of incentives could drive adoption. The scope of that claim is explicitly limited to mathematical reasoning; whether it extends to domains without cheaply checkable answers is left open, and in such domains the false-positive weakness of outcome supervision that makes MATH favorable to process supervision may itself behave differently.

title: LLM Reasoning Series: Process Supervision and Step-Level Reward Models
text:
7 Where This Leads
The paper’s result is that a reward model trained to score each reasoning step ranks correct MATH solutions above incorrect ones more reliably than one trained on final-answer correctness, and that the gap is not an artifact of unequal training sets or final-answer false positives, since it persists under controlled synthetic supervision with clean outcome labels. The mechanism is denser credit assignment: a step-level label tells the model where reasoning fails, which an outcome label does not. Active learning, by surfacing convincing wrong-answer solutions, makes the human labeling that process supervision requires roughly 2.6\times more efficient, and the released PRM800K dataset supplies the step-level labels for further work. The structure — a fixed generator, a learned reward model, and selection over many samples — extends the verifier method of the predecessor work (Cobbe et al. 2021). Whether step-level supervision is worth its labeling cost is a question later work answers in both directions: this paper argues the step-level signal is decisive on MATH, while some subsequent reasoning systems forgo a process reward model entirely in favor of outcome-based rule rewards, reporting that a learned step-scorer is hard to define and prone to reward hacking at scale (DeepSeek-AI et al. 2025).

title: OpenClaw and the Rise of the Agent Runtime
OpenClaw and the Rise of the Agent Runtime
text:
1 Introduction
Most LLM applications still treat the agent as an extension of the chat loop. OpenClaw starts from a different premise: once an agent becomes persistent, tool-using, and multi-surface, the real problem is no longer prompt formatting but runtime design.
That shift is what makes OpenClaw interesting. It is not an operating system in the kernel sense. But it is an always-on agent runtime centered on a Gateway control plane, and it can be usefully understood as an agent-OS-like layer running above the host OS. Rather than optimizing for chat UX first, it shifts the center of gravity toward a persistent runtime: a Gateway that maintains provider connections, exposes a typed WebSocket API, and serves as the shared control plane for clients and nodes across surfaces.
When agents run for multiple steps, the main challenge is no longer just prompting. It becomes a runtime problem: how to route messages, serialize execution, stream tool output coherently, preserve session state, and keep the system operable across multiple interfaces. OpenClaw approaches these concerns as infrastructure problems rather than as prompt-design problems. In that architecture, chat is not the whole system; it is one surface among several, alongside the CLI, web UI, macOS app, and connected nodes.
Capability expansion is handled through skills. OpenClaw snapshots eligible skills when a session starts and reuses that list across turns in the same session for performance. When the skills watcher is enabled, or when a newly eligible remote node appears, that skill list can refresh mid-session and be picked up on the next agent turn.
Compared with dialogue-centered agent setups, OpenClaw looks less like a chat wrapper and more like an operational runtime. The distinctive point is not merely that it can call tools, but that connectivity, session execution, queueing, routing, and tool dispatch are all organized behind a single control plane.

title: OpenClaw and the Rise of the Agent Runtime
section: 2 A von Neumann Metaphor for Agent Systems
text:
2 A von Neumann Metaphor for Agent Systems
The best way to understand this shift is as an architectural metaphor. OpenClaw does not implement a kernel, but it does assume a set of OS-like responsibilities at the agent layer: control, I/O coordination, state continuity, execution governance, and bounded tool access.
At the center sits the Gateway, which functions as both controller and bus. It owns messaging surfaces, accepts WebSocket connections from clients and nodes, validates frames, emits typed events, and uses a structured handshake in which role, device identity, and capabilities are declared up front. That gives OpenClaw a unified control plane for routing, pairing, presence, and command flow across interfaces.
Within that system, the LLM plays the role of the general-purpose inference engine. It is the component that plans, selects tools, and generates responses, while the Gateway and runtime provide the scaffolding that keeps those actions connected to sessions, channels, tools, and policy boundaries. OpenClaw explicitly treats the agent as a managed session with lifecycle control, event handling, prompt customization, persistence, compaction, and model switching.
The memory hierarchy is likewise layered, though only metaphorically. The immediate model context acts like short-term working state; the session runtime preserves active continuity for the turn; and longer-lived workspace files, session artifacts, and diagnostics provide durable state on disk. OpenClaw’s design makes the durable layer unusually explicit by storing memory in Markdown files inside the workspace and treating those files as canonical.
The interfaces around that runtime—CLI, web UI, WebChat, macOS app, and nodes—function like multiplexed I/O surfaces attached to the same computational system. They are not isolated assistants with separate brains; they are different entry points into a shared Gateway-managed runtime.
To expand capabilities, OpenClaw uses skills as modular runtime extensions. Skills are loaded into the session environment and prompt, can be bundled, managed, or workspace-based, and can refresh dynamically under documented conditions. This makes capability growth more composable than relying entirely on one large, hardcoded prompt.
Finally, tools and nodes—local files, browser control, shell execution, APIs, camera, screen recording, location, and other commands—form the agent’s operational environment. OpenClaw’s important move is not simply that the agent can reach those tools, but that access is brought under a common runtime model with pairing, approval, queueing, sandbox options, typed events, and logging.

title: OpenClaw and the Rise of the Agent Runtime
section: 3 The Agentic Loop as a Managed Execution Lifecycle

title: OpenClaw and the Rise of the Agent Runtime
section: 4 Memory and State: Local-First, File-Backed, Auditable
text:
4 Memory and State: Local-First, File-Backed, Auditable
When people build agents, the instinct is often to start with a vector database. OpenClaw takes a more systems-first approach: memory is local-first, file-backed, and human-auditable, while semantic retrieval is layered on top of canonical files rather than replacing them. Memory is plain Markdown in the agent workspace, and those files are the source of truth.

4.1 Markdown-on-Disk as the Source of Truth
OpenClaw memory lives in workspace files, not in an opaque memory service. The model only “remembers” what gets written to disk. This design makes state inspectable, editable, and diffable by ordinary filesystem tools. In practice, it also makes the workspace easy to back up and version.


4.2 Separating Identity from Episodic Memory
OpenClaw also separates bootstrap identity and operating context from recall-oriented memory. In the workspace, it expects user-editable files such as AGENTS.md, SOUL.md, TOOLS.md, IDENTITY.md, and USER.md; during session startup, the template flow directs the agent to read SOUL.md, USER.md, recent daily memory, and, in the main session, MEMORY.md. This creates a practical distinction between always-present operating context and selectively accumulated memory.


4.3 Privacy Boundaries as a First-Class Rule
That separation is paired with an explicit privacy rule. MEMORY.md, the curated long-term memory file, is loaded only in the main private session and never in group contexts. This materially reduces the chance that long-term personal context is injected into shared channels by default.


4.4 Vector Search is a Derived Capability
OpenClaw does support semantic and hybrid retrieval, but the retrieval layer is deliberately downstream of the files themselves. The memory plugin provides search and retrieval functions, and the system supports hybrid search, reranking, temporal weighting, and optional vector acceleration. The important design point is that the index is derived from Markdown rather than replacing Markdown as the canonical store.


4.5 Pluggable Retrieval Backends
Because the files remain canonical, OpenClaw can vary the retrieval backend without changing the memory format. That keeps storage and retrieval decoupled and makes the system more operable for teams that care about inspectability over black-box persistence.
This memory design is one of OpenClaw’s clearest systems choices. Critical identity and behavioral context live in explicit workspace files; episodic and durable recall live in Markdown memory layers; and semantic retrieval is an optional acceleration layer rather than the core substrate.
That tradeoff is significant. It favors inspectability and operational trust over the illusion of “magical memory,” which is often harder to debug, harder to govern, and harder to recover when things go wrong.

title: OpenClaw and the Rise of the Agent Runtime
text:
5 Conclusion
The shift from a conversational wrapper to a runtime-centric design is not merely aesthetic. OpenClaw centralizes connectivity through the Gateway, serializes agent execution by session lane, exposes queue modes that can steer or defer input, and anchors longer-lived memory in auditable workspace files. Together, those choices target the operational friction that appears once agents become persistent, tool-using, and multi-surface.
Just as importantly, this runtime discipline creates cleaner operational traces. Because OpenClaw separates lifecycle events, assistant output, tool events, queueing behavior, session state, and usage telemetry, it appears well suited to collecting structured agent trajectories. That does not mean the project officially positions itself as an RLHF or post-training framework; rather, it suggests that OpenClaw provides a promising substrate for future preference-learning or reinforcement-learning-style work on end-to-end agent behavior.
Frameworks remain excellent for prototyping agent logic. But operating agents across real tools, real sessions, and real interfaces requires governance, observability, and state you can actually inspect. OpenClaw’s significance is that it pushes those concerns into the runtime itself and treats them as first-class system design problems.

title: LLM Alignment Series: Direct Preference Optimization
LLM Alignment Series: Direct Preference Optimization
text:
1 Introduction
Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is designed to replace the preference-learning stage of RLHF after supervised fine-tuning. More concretely, it compresses the usual two-step procedure—first training a reward model, and then optimizing the policy with an RL algorithm such as PPO (Schulman et al. 2017) into a single-stage method that trains the policy directly on preference pairs. The paper (Rafailov et al. 2024) begins by reviewing the standard three-stage RLHF pipeline, consisting of supervised fine-tuning, reward modeling, and RL-based policy optimization, and then proposes DPO as an alternative that does not require explicit reward-model training or reinforcement learning in the usual sense. Instead, the policy is optimized directly from preference data .
The motivation comes from several practical weaknesses of standard RLHF. The first is pipeline complexity: traditional RLHF requires multiple models and additional optimization machinery, making it substantially more complicated than ordinary supervised learning. The second is training instability: the paper explicitly describes RLHF as a complex and often unstable procedure, and notes that actor-critic and PPO-style methods can suffer from high-variance updates and unstable dynamics. The third is computational cost: standard RLHF requires sampling from the current language-model policy inside the training loop, which is expensive, whereas DPO avoids this online sampling step. The fourth is engineering burden: RLHF typically involves substantial hyperparameter tuning and implementation overhead, while DPO is presented as a simpler, more stable, and more lightweight alternative.
In summary, DPO replaces the entire “reward model + PPO” back half of RLHF with a direct preference-optimization objective. Its key move is to rewrite the original RLHF objective into a simple binary cross-entropy style loss, so that the policy can be learned directly from pairwise preference data.

title: LLM Alignment Series: Direct Preference Optimization
text:
2 DPO v.s. PPO
The central claim of DPO is not that it approximates PPO. Rather, under a particular preference-model assumption, it optimizes the same KL-constrained RLHF objective in an equivalent way, while avoiding both explicit reward-model training and the reinforcement-learning loop.
In the standard RLHF pipeline, the second stage proceeds in two steps. One first fits a reward model, and then uses an RL algorithm such as PPO to optimize the policy under a KL regularization term:

\max_\pi \; \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi(\cdot \mid x)}[r(x,y)] - \beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi(\cdot \mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot \mid x)).

DPO starts from this same KL-constrained reward-maximization objective. Its key theoretical step is to use the closed-form expression of the optimal policy under this objective:

\pi_r(y \mid x) \propto \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)\exp\!\left(\frac{r(x,y)}{\beta}\right).

This expression shows that the reward can be reparameterized in terms of the log-ratio between the policy and the reference policy. Once this change of variables is made, and once preferences are modeled with a Bradley–Terry model, the original RLHF objective can be rewritten as a direct binary cross-entropy objective on preference pairs. The result is that the policy can be trained directly, without separately fitting a reward model and without running PPO or any other online RL algorithm.
PPO is one RL-based algorithm for optimizing the KL-constrained objective. DPO is a direct policy optimization method obtained by rewriting that same objective through a change of variables. For this reason, the paper does not present DPO as an approximation to PPO. Instead, it argues that the two methods optimize the same underlying objective, but follow different optimization routes.

title: LLM Alignment Series: Direct Preference Optimization
section: 3 Soft Value Function , Baseline, and Advantage
text:
3 Soft Value Function , Baseline, and Advantage
This point can be understood at three closely related levels. The paper gives the optimal policy for the KL-constrained RLHF objective:

\pi_r(y \mid x) = \frac{1}{Z(x)} \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)\exp(r(x,y)/\beta),

where

Z(x) = \sum_y \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)\exp(r(x,y)/\beta).

Later, the PPO-side derivation contains the term

\beta \log \sum_y \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)\exp(r_\phi(x,y)/\beta).

The paper explicitly interprets this normalization term as the soft value function under the reference policy \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. It is called a value function because it depends only on the prompt x and aggregates, for that prompt, the overall attainable quality across all possible completions. It is called soft because the aggregation is not an ordinary maximum, but a log-sum-exp. This is the same structural object that appears in maximum-entropy RL and control-as-inference, where one writes

V(s) = \alpha \log \sum_a \exp(Q(s,a)/\alpha).

The only difference here is that the completions are additionally weighted by the reference policy \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x). Intuitively, r(x,y) is the score of one particular completion, while

\beta \log \sum_y \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)\exp(r(x,y)/\beta)

represents the overall attainable score level for the prompt as a whole. In that sense, it behaves like a state-level value rather than an action-level value.
This immediately leads to the analogy with advantage functions. In standard RL, one distinguishes among Q(s,a), which measures the value of taking a particular action, V(s), which measures the overall value of the state, and A(s,a)=Q(s,a)-V(s), which measures how much better a given action is than the state average. The same analogy applies here. The completion-level reward r_\phi(x,y) plays the role of a Q-like score, while the normalization term plays the role of a soft value V(x). Their difference therefore measures how much better a completion is relative to the overall level of that prompt. Although the paper does not explicitly name this quantity an advantage, the interpretation is very close:

\underbrace{r_\phi(x,y)}_{\text{Q-like}}
\;-\;
\underbrace{\beta \log \sum_y \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)\exp(r_\phi(x,y)/\beta)}_{\text{soft }V(x)}.

This is naturally viewed as a soft advantage.
The same term is also a baseline in the policy-gradient sense. In policy-gradient methods, any quantity that depends only on the state, or here only on the prompt x, can be used as a baseline. Such a term does not change the optimal solution, but it can substantially reduce gradient variance. The normalization term has exactly this property: it depends on x but not on the sampled completion y. That is why the paper notes that this term does not affect the optimal solution, but that omitting it can lead to high-variance policy gradients. It can therefore be handled using a learned value function, or approximated by a completion baseline. DPO avoids this difficulty through reparameterization.
The reason variance increases without this term is also intuitive. If one directly uses r_\phi(x,y) in the policy gradient, then the gradient mixes together two kinds of signal: the relative quality of the sampled completion, and the prompt-level offset induced by the overall scale of rewards under that prompt. What one really wants to know is not whether a completion has a high absolute reward, but whether it is better than other plausible completions for the same prompt. The normalization term performs exactly this centering or calibration step. With it, the update behaves more like advantage learning. Without it, prompt-level common offsets remain inside the gradient and increase variance.
This is precisely where DPO becomes especially elegant. The paper rewrites the reward as

r(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)} + \beta \log Z(x),

where \beta \log Z(x) is exactly the normalization term discussed above. However, under the Bradley–Terry preference model, DPO only depends on reward differences. When comparing a chosen response y_w and a rejected response y_l, one forms

r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l),

and the term \beta \log Z(x) cancels exactly because it depends only on x. As a result, DPO does not need to estimate this soft value or baseline explicitly. This is why PPO or actor-critic style methods require a baseline or value function to accommodate the term, whereas DPO makes it disappear automatically through pairwise reward differences.
In one sentence, this normalization term is called a soft value function because it is the log-sum-exp aggregate value of all completions under a prompt; it behaves like a baseline because it depends only on the prompt and can be subtracted to reduce variance; and it corresponds to advantage because reward minus this soft value is, in effect, a soft advantage.

3.1 Why the Baseline Does Not Change the Expected Gradient
It is helpful to rewrite Eq. 10 in the paper for a fixed prompt x. Define the prompt-conditioned objective as

J_x(\theta)
=
\mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)}
\left[
r_\phi(x,y)
-
f(x)
-
\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)}
\right],

where

f(x)
=
\beta \log \sum_y \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)\exp(r_\phi(x,y)/\beta).

The paper interprets it as the soft value function under the reference policy, and notes that without it, the policy gradient can have high variance. The key structural fact is that f(x) depends only on the prompt x, not on the sampled completion y. For that reason, it is a standard state-dependent, or here prompt-dependent, baseline.
To see why such a baseline does not change the expected gradient, begin by differentiating the objective:

\nabla_\theta J_x
=
\nabla_\theta
\sum_y
\pi_\theta(y \mid x)
\left[
r_\phi(x,y)-f(x)-\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)}
\right].

Let

A_\theta(x,y)
=
r_\phi(x,y)-f(x)-\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)}.

Then

\nabla_\theta J_x
=
\sum_y \nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(y \mid x) A_\theta(x,y)
+
\sum_y \pi_\theta(y \mid x)\nabla_\theta A_\theta(x,y).

Since r_\phi(x,y), f(x), and \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x) do not depend on \theta, only the \log \pi_\theta(y \mid x) term contributes to \nabla_\theta A_\theta(x,y). Therefore,

\nabla_\theta A_\theta(x,y)
=
-\beta \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y \mid x).

Using the identity

\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(y \mid x)
=
\pi_\theta(y \mid x)\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y \mid x),

we obtain

\nabla_\theta J_x
=
\mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi_\theta}
\left[
A_\theta(x,y)\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y \mid x)
\right]
-
\beta
\mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi_\theta}
\left[
\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y \mid x)
\right].

The second expectation vanishes because

\mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi_\theta}
[\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y \mid x)]
=
\sum_y \pi_\theta(y \mid x)\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y \mid x)
=
\sum_y \nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(y \mid x)
=
\nabla_\theta \sum_y \pi_\theta(y \mid x)
=
\nabla_\theta 1
=
0.

Thus the gradient reduces to

\nabla_\theta J_x
=
\mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi_\theta}
\left[
\left(
r_\phi(x,y)-f(x)-\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)}
\right)
\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y \mid x)
\right].

Now isolate the contribution of the baseline term f(x). Since it does not depend on y, we have

\mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi_\theta}
\left[
f(x)\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y \mid x)
\right]
=
f(x)
\mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi_\theta}
[\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y \mid x)]
=
f(x)\cdot 0
=
0.

This is the fundamental reason a baseline does not change the expected gradient. As long as it depends only on the prompt and not on the sampled completion, its contribution disappears in expectation after multiplication by the score function \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y \mid x).


3.2 Why the Baseline Changes the Variance
Although the expected gradient is unchanged, the per-sample gradient is changed. Without the baseline, the single-sample gradient has the form

g(y)
=
\left(
r_\phi(x,y)-\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)}
\right)
\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y \mid x).

With the baseline f(x) included, it becomes

g_b(y)
=
\left(
r_\phi(x,y)-f(x)-\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)}
\right)
\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y \mid x).

These two random variables have the same mean, but in general they do not have the same variance:

\mathrm{Var}[g_b(y)] \neq \mathrm{Var}[g(y)].

The intuition is that the baseline removes the prompt-level common offset shared by all completions for the same prompt. Without this subtraction, the gradient weight mixes together several effects: the overall difficulty of the prompt, the overall reward level of the completion set under that prompt, and the relative quality of the sampled completion compared with competing completions. What one really wants for stable policy optimization is mainly the third component. The baseline suppresses the first two by centering the signal. As a result, the gradient becomes closer to a relative-improvement signal and its sample-to-sample fluctuation is reduced.
This also explains why the term

r_\phi(x,y)-f(x)

is naturally viewed as an advantage-like quantity. The reward r_\phi(x,y) plays the role of a completion-level Q-like score, while f(x) plays the role of a prompt-level soft value. Their difference measures how much better a completion is than the overall level associated with that prompt. In RL language, the word value emphasizes its state-level role, the word baseline emphasizes its variance-reduction role in policy gradients, and the word advantage emphasizes the centered difference structure. These are three views of the same mathematical object.


3.3 Why This Matters in PPO-Style RLHF
This issue is especially important in PPO-style RLHF because the action space is extremely large and the sampling noise is already substantial. If each sampled completion carries a large prompt-dependent offset in its gradient weight, the updates can become highly unstable. That is why the paper emphasizes that omitting the normalization term leads to high-variance policy gradients. In practice, one can try to learn a value function to approximate this term, or use a completion baseline, but both introduce additional estimation and engineering burden.
A more compact way to express this is to define

w(y)
=
r_\phi(x,y)-\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)},
\qquad
s(y)
=
\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y \mid x).

Then the one-sample gradient takes the form

(w(y)-b(x))s(y).

For fixed x, a well-chosen baseline b(x) reduces the spread of this product. In classical policy-gradient theory, the optimal scalar baseline is a weighted average return under the score-function norm. Here, the paper points out that the normalization term in Eq. 10 provides exactly such a meaningful soft value or baseline.


3.4 Why DPO Avoids the Baseline Problem
This is where the DPO reparameterization becomes especially elegant. The paper rewrites the reward as

r(x,y)
=
\beta \log \frac{\pi(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)}
+
\beta \log Z(x),

where \beta \log Z(x) is precisely the normalization term discussed above. Under the Bradley–Terry preference model, however, DPO depends only on reward differences. When comparing a chosen response y_w and a rejected response y_l, one forms

r(x,y_w)-r(x,y_l),

and the term \beta \log Z(x) cancels exactly because it depends only on the prompt x. As a result, DPO never needs to estimate this soft value or baseline explicitly. This is why the paper states that the DPO reparameterization yields a reward representation that does not require baselines.
In one sentence, the baseline does not change the expected gradient because it depends only on the prompt and therefore has zero expectation when multiplied by \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta; it reduces variance because it removes prompt-level common offsets and leaves behind a more advantage-like relative-improvement signal.

title: LLM Alignment Series: Direct Preference Optimization
section: 4 DPO Is Not Just a Generic Pairwise Ranking Loss
text:
4 DPO Is Not Just a Generic Pairwise Ranking Loss
At the level of surface form, the DPO objective is indeed a pairwise logistic, or binary cross-entropy, loss. However, it should not be understood as an ordinary pairwise ranking loss. What it ranks is not an arbitrary score function, but a quantity with a precise RLHF interpretation: an implicit reward defined relative to a reference policy. Equivalently, it can be viewed as a reference-adjusted, advantage-like margin.
To see the distinction, it is useful to begin with the standard pairwise ranking objective:

-\log \sigma\big(s_\theta(x,y_w)-s_\theta(x,y_l)\big).

Here, s_\theta(x,y) is just an unconstrained scoring function. The objective only says that the chosen response should receive a higher score than the rejected one. This is sufficient for ranking, but it does not specify what the score means. It may be a heuristic ranking score with no principled relation to the KL-constrained RLHF objective, the reference policy, or the closed-form optimal policy.
DPO is different because its score is not introduced arbitrarily. Instead, it is derived from the KL-constrained RLHF objective. Starting from the optimal policy form, the reward can be reparameterized as

r(x,y)
=
\beta \log \frac{\pi(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)}
+
\beta \log Z(x).

Under the Bradley–Terry preference model, only reward differences matter. As a result, the prompt-dependent term \beta \log Z(x) cancels in pairwise comparisons, and the preference probability becomes

p^*(y_w \succ y_l \mid x)
=
\sigma\left(
\beta \log \frac{\pi^*(y_w \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w \mid x)}
-
\beta \log \frac{\pi^*(y_l \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l \mid x)}
\right).

This leads to the DPO loss

L_{\mathrm{DPO}}
=
-\log \sigma\left(
\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w \mid x)}
-
\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l \mid x)}
\right).

The quantity being compared is therefore

\hat r_\theta(x,y)
=
\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)},

which the paper interprets as an implicit reward induced by the language model. In other words, DPO is not merely learning that the chosen response should have a higher arbitrary score. It is learning that the chosen response should have a higher reference-adjusted implicit reward than the rejected one.
This is also why the DPO objective is naturally connected to an advantage-like interpretation. Recall that the original reward decomposition contains a prompt-dependent normalization term:

r(x,y)
=
\beta \log \frac{\pi(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)}
+
\beta \log Z(x).

The second term depends only on the prompt and behaves like a soft value function or baseline. When one forms the pairwise difference,

r(x,y_w)-r(x,y_l)
=
\beta \log \frac{\pi(y_w \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w \mid x)}
-
\beta \log \frac{\pi(y_l \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l \mid x)},

the baseline disappears. What remains is not an absolute reward, but a relative, normalized comparison between completions under the same prompt. For that reason, DPO can be viewed as learning whether the chosen response has a positive advantage-like margin over the rejected response, and how large that margin is.
This reference adjustment is essential. If one removed the reference policy and wrote instead

-\log \sigma\big(\log \pi_\theta(y_w \mid x)-\log \pi_\theta(y_l \mid x)\big),

the objective would reduce to a much more naive pairwise likelihood-pushing rule: increase the probability of preferred responses and decrease the probability of dispreferred ones. DPO does not do this. It compares

\log \pi_\theta(y \mid x)-\log \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x),

which measures how much additional preference the current policy assigns to a completion relative to the reference policy. This is precisely how KL information is encoded into the objective. The result is a ranking-like loss with reference anchoring, KL semantics, and a reward interpretation, rather than a generic ranking surrogate.
The gradient makes this margin-sensitive behavior even clearer. The paper writes the DPO gradient as

\nabla_\theta L_{\mathrm{DPO}}
=
-\beta \,\mathbb{E}\left[
\sigma\big(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w)\big)
\big(\nabla \log \pi_\theta(y_w \mid x)-\nabla \log \pi_\theta(y_l \mid x)\big)
\right].

This form shows that DPO is not only learning the correct ordering. The update magnitude also depends on how severely the implicit reward model misorders the pair. If the chosen response already has a much larger implicit reward than the rejected one, the update becomes small. If the rejected response is incorrectly favored, the update becomes large. This is the behavior of a margin-sensitive correction rule, not merely a binary ordering rule.
The most accurate summary is therefore the following. In form, DPO uses a pairwise logistic loss. In meaning, it performs maximum-likelihood learning on the implicit reward difference induced by the KL-constrained RLHF objective. Because this difference is reference-adjusted and baseline-cancelled, it is best understood as an advantage-like margin rather than an arbitrary ranking score.
The ordinary pairwise ranking learns which response should score higher, whereas DPO learns which response is better in reference-relative implicit reward, and by how much.

title: LLM Alignment Series: Direct Preference Optimization
text:
5 Sequence-Level v.s. Token-Level Advantage
The reference-adjusted log-ratio in DPO can be understood as a sequence-level, reference-relative, soft-baseline-canceled advantage signal. At the same time, it should not be confused with the token-level advantage used in traditional reinforcement learning.
The paper defines the implicit reward as

\hat r_\theta(x,y)
=
\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)},

and interprets the normalization term in Eq. 10 of the paper (Rafailov et al. 2024) as a soft value function under the reference policy. Because the DPO objective depends only on reward differences, this prompt-dependent normalization term cancels out, leaving a quantity that is naturally interpreted relative to a baseline.

5.1 Why It Can Be Viewed as an Advantage
In reinforcement learning, an advantage measures how much better an action is compared to a baseline or state value. DPO admits a closely related decomposition. The reparameterized reward takes the form

r(x,y)
=
\beta \log \frac{\pi(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)}
+
\beta \log Z(x),

where \beta \log Z(x) depends only on the prompt and behaves like a soft value or baseline. The remaining term,

\beta \log \frac{\pi(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)},

measures how much additional preference the policy assigns to a completion relative to the reference policy. This can be interpreted as a gain over a reference distribution, and therefore resembles an advantage-like quantity.


5.2 Pairwise Advantage Margin in DPO
Under the Bradley–Terry preference model, only reward differences are relevant. When comparing a chosen response y_w and a rejected response y_l, the baseline term cancels:

r(x,y_w)-r(x,y_l)
=
\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w \mid x)}
-
\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l \mid x)}.

As a result, DPO does not compare absolute scores, but relative gains under the same prompt. The objective asks which completion is more preferred relative to the reference policy, and by how much. This is why the signal behaves like a pairwise advantage margin: it captures both the sign of preference and the magnitude of the margin.
Despite this analogy, the DPO signal is fundamentally different from the token-level advantage used in actor-critic methods.
First, it is sequence-level. Both \pi_\theta(y \mid x) and \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x) are probabilities over entire completions. The DPO loss is defined over full sequences, not individual tokens. Although sequence probabilities can be decomposed into sums of token log-probabilities in practice, the theoretical object remains a completion-level quantity rather than a per-step signal.
Second, it is not derived from Bellman or temporal-difference structure. In standard RL, advantages such as A_t = Q_t - V_t depend on state transitions, future return decomposition, and often bootstrapped value estimates. DPO does not involve this form of credit assignment. Instead, it starts from the closed-form optimal policy of a KL-constrained objective, performs a change of variables, and learns from offline preference pairs. The reward signal is implicit and static, rather than recursively defined.
Third, it is reference-relative rather than purely state-relative. A traditional advantage answers the question: how much better is this action than the average outcome under the current state. In contrast, the DPO signal answers: how much more preference does the current policy assign to this completion relative to a fixed reference policy. This reference anchoring encodes the KL constraint directly into the signal. Without it, the objective would collapse into a naive pairwise likelihood adjustment without the intended RLHF semantics.
The difference is also evident in the gradient structure. The DPO gradient is weighted by

\sigma\big(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w)\big),

which increases when the model incorrectly assigns higher implicit reward to the rejected response. The update then simultaneously increases the likelihood of the chosen response and decreases that of the rejected one. This is a correction of sequence-level pairwise ordering errors, not a token-level adjustment guided by per-step advantages.
In summary, the reference-adjusted log-ratio behaves like an advantage because it measures the gain of a completion relative to a baseline induced by the reference policy. However, it is not equivalent to a traditional token-level advantage. It is a sequence-level, pairwise, offline preference-based margin defined through implicit rewards, rather than a Bellman-style, stepwise credit assignment signal. DPO learns which completion is more preferable relative to a reference policy, whereas standard RL advantage learning evaluates how each action compares to the expected value at a given state.

title: LLM Alignment Series: The Policy Gradient Theorem
LLM Alignment Series: The Policy Gradient Theorem
text:
1 Introduction
InstructGPT (Ouyang et al. 2022), a direct precursor to ChatGPT’s RLHF methodology, used Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) (Schulman et al. 2017) with a KL-to-reference constraint to perform online policy optimization against a preference-trained reward model. PPO has since become a cornerstone of the GenAI era.
PPO is a policy-gradient method that updates a parameterized policy via stochastic gradient ascent to increase expected reward, but it is engineered to avoid the dominant failure mode of vanilla policy gradients: overly large steps that induce policy drift and abrupt performance collapse under noisy advantage estimates and scarce on-policy data. Its “proximal” idea is to constrain each update so the new policy cannot move too far from the old policy on sampled actions, keeping improvements incremental and reliable.
But to truly grasp how PPO calculates these updates and why it requires constraints, we must first understand the mathematical engine driving it: the fundamental Policy Gradient Theorem.
The Policy Gradient Theorem involves a lot of moving parts. Before we dive into the derivations, keep this notation glossary handy to help you track the variables, spaces, and probability distributions.


Notation Glossary (Click to expand)


1.1 Spaces, States, and Actions







Notation
Description




\mathcal{S}
The state space (the set of all possible states in the environment).


\mathcal{A}
The action space (the set of all possible actions the agent can take).


s, s', s''
Specific, concrete states within the environment.


S_t
A random variable representing the state at a specific time step t.


s_t
A specific, observed state value at time step t in a sample.


s_0, S_0
The initial state (s_0 as a concrete value, S_0 as a random variable).


a
A specific action taken by the agent.


t
A discrete time step in the environment.


\tau
A realized trajectory or sampled sequence of interactions: \{s_0, a_0, r_1, s_1, \dots\}.





1.2 Functions and Parameters







Notation
Description




\theta
The learnable parameters of the neural network (or function approximator) defining the policy.


V^\pi(s)
The state-value function; the expected return starting from state s and following policy \pi.


Q^\pi(s, a)
The action-value function; the expected return starting from state s, taking action a, and then following policy \pi.


r(s, a)
The immediate reward received by the agent after taking action a in state s.


J(\theta)
The overall objective function to be maximized (the expected return of the policy).


\phi(s)
The local policy improvement term at state s, defined as the sum of policy gradients weighted by action-values.





1.3 Probabilities and Distributions







Notation
Description




\pi
The policy followed by the agent.


\pi(a \mid s)
The probability of taking action a when in state s, according to policy \pi.


P(s' \mid s, a)
The environment’s transition probability of moving to state s' after taking action a in state s. This is the transition model (or system dynamics) of the Markov Decision Process (MDP). It belongs entirely to the environment and has absolutely nothing to do with the agent’s policy.


P(s \to s')
The transition probability of moving from state s to s' under the current behavior of policy \pi. This is the state-to-state transition probability under a specific policy \pi. It combines the agent’s decision-making with the environment’s physics.


\mu_0(s_0)
The probability distribution of the starting state s_0.


\mu_\pi(s)
The discounted state visitation distribution (or unnormalized frequency) indicating how much time the agent spends in state s under policy \pi.


\text{Pr}(S_t = s \mid s_0, \pi)
The exact probability of the agent being in state s at time step t, given it started at s_0 and follows policy \pi.

title: LLM Alignment Series: The Policy Gradient Theorem
text:
2 Bellman Equation
The Bellman Equation (Sutton and Barto 2018) for the state-value function V^\pi(s) is the expected value of all possible actions taken from that state:
V^\pi(s) = \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \pi(a|s) Q^\pi(s, a)
When we apply the gradient operator \nabla_\theta to both sides of this equation, we use the product rule (Leibniz rule) because both the policy \pi(a|s) and the action-value function Q^\pi(s, a) are functions of the policy parameters \theta:
\nabla_{\theta} V^{\pi}(s) = \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \left[ \nabla_{\theta} \pi(a|s) Q^{\pi}(s, a) + \pi(a|s) \nabla_{\theta} Q^{\pi}(s, a) \right] \tag{1}
The Bellman equation for the action-value function Q^\pi(s, a) is:
Q^{\pi}(s, a) = r(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s' \in \mathcal{S}} P(s'|s, a) V^{\pi}(s')
This equation defines the value of taking a specific action a in state s as the immediate reward r(s, a) plus the discounted expected value of the resulting next state s'. When we apply the gradient operator \nabla_{\theta} to this expression, the immediate reward r(s, a) and the environment’s transition probabilities P(s'|s, a) are treated as constants because they do not depend on the policy parameters \theta.
Consequently, the gradient passes through the summation and the transition model, focusing entirely on the change in the future state-value function \nabla_{\theta} V^{\pi}(s'):
\nabla_{\theta} Q^{\pi}(s, a) = \nabla_{\theta} \left( r(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s' \in \mathcal{S}} P(s'|s, a) V^{\pi}(s') \right) = \gamma \sum_{s' \in \mathcal{S}} P(s'|s, a) \nabla_{\theta} V^{\pi}(s') \tag{2}
Substituting Equation 2 back into the original expression Equation 1 reveals a recursive structure:
\nabla_{\theta} V^{\pi}(s) = \underbrace{\sum_{a} \nabla_{\theta} \pi(a|s) Q^{\pi}(s, a)}_{\phi(s)} + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s \to s') \nabla_{\theta} V^{\pi}(s') \tag{3} Here, P(s \to s') represents the transition probability from state s to s' under the current policy \pi. Replace the \nabla_\theta V^\pi(s') on the right side with its own definition Equation 3, we have: \nabla_\theta V^\pi(s) = \phi(s) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s \to s') \left[ \phi(s') + \gamma \sum_{s''} P(s' \to s'') \nabla_\theta V^\pi(s'') \right] By distributing the transition probability across the terms of the recursive expansion, the relationship between the state-space summations and the time-indexed expectations becomes clear:
\nabla_\theta V^\pi(s) = \phi(s) + \gamma \underbrace{\sum_{s'} P(s \to s') \phi(s')}_{\mathbb{E}_\pi[\phi(S_1) \mid s]} + \gamma^2 \underbrace{\sum_{s'} \sum_{s''} P(s \to s') P(s' \to s'') \phi(s'')}_{\mathbb{E}_\pi[\phi(S_2) \mid s]} + \dots \tag{4}
This expansion demonstrates how the value function gradient at state s is constructed from the immediate local improvement and the discounted sum of expected future improvements. The terms under the brackets identify that the summation over all possible next states s' is the mathematical definition of the expectation over the random variable S_1, while the nested summation over s'' represents the expectation over S_2. By viewing the derivation this way, it is evident that the gradient at any single point is a cumulative measure of all potential future policy updates along every possible path the agent might take.

Side note: To calculate P(s \to s'), you have to sum up the probabilities of every possible action the agent could take in state s, multiplied by the environment’s probability of moving to s' given that specific action. Mathematically, P(s \to s') is the marginalization of P(s' \mid s, a) over the policy \pi:
P(s \to s') = \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \pi(a \mid s) P(s' \mid s, a) This shows exactly why P(s \to s') shifts whenever you update the policy parameters \theta, whereas P(s' \mid s, a) remains rigidly fixed for the entire training process!

title: LLM Alignment Series: The Policy Gradient Theorem
section: 3 From a Time-based View to a State-based View
text:
3 From a Time-based View to a State-based View
The core “magic” of the policy gradient theorem is the conceptual shift from tracking an agent’s individual steps through time (t=0, 1, 2, \dots) to observing the aggregate density of the agent’s presence across the environment’s state space (s \in \mathcal{S}). It proves that we do not need to calculate an infinite series of future effects for every specific moment in time. Instead, we can simply look at the global state visitation distribution \mu_\pi(s)—the state-based view—to determine how to update our policy parameters \theta.
The time-based view (forward perspective) describes the gradient as the expected sum of all future local policy “nudges” \phi(S_t), discounted by \gamma^t, starting from the initial state s_0. It focuses on the sequential trajectory of the agent.
The state-based view (stationary perspective) collapses the time dimension into the stationary distribution \mu_\pi(s). It treats the gradient as a simple weighted average of the local improvements \phi(s) over the entire state space, which is what allows us to train using a buffer of sampled transitions.
To clarify the notation, we use S_t (uppercase) for the random variable and s_t (lowercase) for the specific value observed in a sample. The sampled sequence is a realized trajectory \tau = \{s_0, a_0, r_1, s_1, \dots\}.

3.1 The Time-based View
The goal of the agent is to maximize its expected return from the moment it begins interacting with the environment. We formally define this objective function J(\theta) as the expected value of the state-value function over the initial state distribution:
J(\theta) \triangleq \mathbb{E}_{s_0 \sim \mu_0}[V^\pi(s_0)]
Writing this expectation explicitly as a sum over all possible initial states s_0, weighted by their starting probability \mu_0(s_0), gives us the starting point for our derivation:
J(\theta) = \sum_{s_0} \mu_0(s_0) V^{\pi}(s_0) Before moving further, it is worth pausing to clarify the notation \mu_0. The subscript 0 explicitly refers to the time step t=0, denoting the environment’s initial state distribution. This distinction is necessary because the very first state an agent encounters is typically determined entirely by the environment’s reset mechanics, independent of the agent’s behavior. We use the 0 subscript to isolate this localized starting point from the subsequent trajectory. This directly contrasts with \mu_\pi(s), which appears in the state-based view (stationary perspective). While \mu_0 only captures the isolated snapshot at the exact moment an episode begins, \mu_\pi(s) is the discounted state visitation distribution that aggregates the probability of visiting a state across all future time steps (t=0, 1, 2, \dots). Unlike the starting state, this global distribution is continuously shaped by the agent’s active policy \pi.
We begin with the gradient of the objective J(\theta), which is the weighted sum of the gradients of the values of the initial states s_0: \nabla_{\theta} J(\theta) = \sum_{s_0} \mu_0(s_0) \nabla_{\theta} V^{\pi}(s_0) As established in the recursive unrolling of the Bellman equation in Equation 4, \nabla_{\theta} V^{\pi}(s_0) is equal to the discounted sum of all future local policy improvements \phi(\cdot) that the agent will encounter: \nabla_{\theta} J(\theta) = \sum_{s_0} \mu_0(s_0) \left[ \phi(s_0) + \gamma \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\phi(S_1) \mid s_0] + \gamma^2 \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\phi(S_2) \mid s_0] + \dots \right] Note that s_0 is the specific value we are summing over. S_1 is the random variable (the unknown future). We are iterating through every possible concrete state in the state space \mathcal{S} and weighting the result by the probability \mu_0(s_0). When we are “inside” a summation, we are usually dealing with a specific, fixed value for that iteration.However, the starting point of the process, considered as a concept, is a random variable S_0.


3.2 The State-based View
To see how the “collapse” happens, we write out the expectations as explicit sums over all possible states s that could be visited at each time step t:
\nabla_{\theta} J(\theta) = \sum_{s_0} \mu_0(s_0) \sum_{t=0}^\infty \gamma^t \sum_{s} \text{Pr}(S_t = s \mid s_0, \pi) \phi(s)
The mathematical “miracle” occurs when we swap the order of the summations for t and s. Instead of tracking what happens at each second of the agent’s life, we look at each state s in the environment and ask how much total discounted weight it accumulates across all possible times: \nabla_{\theta} J(\theta) = \sum_{s} \left[ \sum_{s_0} \mu_0(s_0) \sum_{t=0}^\infty \gamma^t \text{Pr}(S_t = s \mid s_0, \pi) \right] \phi(s) \tag{5} The expression inside the brackets is exactly the definition of the discounted state visitation distribution \mu_\pi(s). It represents the total discounted probability of visiting state s over an infinite horizon, given the starting distribution \mu_0 and the behavior of policy \pi: \mu_\pi(s) = \sum_{s_0} \mu_0(s_0) \sum_{t=0}^\infty \gamma^t \text{Pr}(S_t = s \mid s_0, \pi) In the formula, S_t is the random variable representing the state at time t, and the sum over s_0 accounts for the probability of starting in various initial states according to the distribution \mu_0. This expression represents the unnormalized discounted state visitation frequency, which measures the total expected discounted time an agent spends in state s over an infinite horizon. Unlike a standard probability distribution that sums to one, the sum of this measure over the entire state space \mathcal{S} equals 1/(1-\gamma), reflecting the total discounted time available in the process. When using this unnormalized form in the policy gradient theorem, the gradient \nabla_{\theta} J(\theta) is expressed as a direct sum \sum_{s} \mu_{\pi}(s) \phi(s), effectively accumulating every local policy improvement throughout the agent’s lifetime. If a normalized probability distribution is required for an expectation, this frequency is typically multiplied by (1-\gamma) to ensure the weights sum to unity.
By substituting \mu_\pi(s) back into Equation 5, the infinite time series collapses into a single, elegant spatial weighting: \nabla_{\theta} J(\theta) = \sum_{s} \mu_\pi(s) \phi(s) \tag{6}
This result is fundamental because it proves that the complex, indirect effect of the policy on the future state distribution is already captured by simply weighting the local gradients by the current visitation frequency. We do not need to compute the derivative of the distribution itself; we only need to sample from it. As established in the recursive unrolling, the total gradient of the objective J(\theta) is the sum of these local improvements across all states, weighted by the discounted visitation frequency \mu_\pi(s).
